destinations.name: Hong Kong
destinations.summary: World-class transit and skyline views at mainland-beating prices, but a March 2026 law now lets police demand your phone password at the border, and it is not a bluff.
destinations.headline: Hong Kong in 2026: the transit is unbeatable, the harbour view is free, and yes, they can make you unlock your phone
destinations.body:
Hong Kong still runs on the best urban transit system most travelers will ever use, and none of it requires guesswork. An adult On-Loan Octopus card costs HK$150 at any MTR Customer Service Centre, including the one inside Hong Kong International Airport, which breaks down as a HK$50 refundable deposit plus HK$100 of starting balance. Visitors who do not want to deal with a deposit refund can instead buy a no-deposit Tourist Octopus for HK$39. Single MTR and bus fares run roughly HK$3 to HK$30 depending on distance, and paying with Octopus is consistently cheaper than buying single-journey paper tickets. The Airport Express into town costs HK$130 to Hong Kong Station at the counter, or HK$120 with an Octopus card, with cheaper stops at Kowloon Station (HK$115, or HK$105 with Octopus) and Tsing Yi (HK$80, or HK$73 with Octopus).

Entry itself has gotten simpler on paper. Hong Kong eliminated arrival and departure card requirements entirely on October 16, 2024, for all travelers, and immigration now processes entries using airline-submitted passenger information instead. Visa-free access covers roughly 170 countries, with US, Canadian, Australian, New Zealand, and most EU passport holders getting up to 90 days, UK citizens getting a notably generous 180 days, and Indian passport holders getting 14 days but only after completing a free online Pre-Arrival Registration, whose minimum applicant age dropped from 11 to 7 as of January 19, 2026.

The real 2026 story, though, is a legal change that has nothing to do with queues or fares. On March 23, 2026, Hong Kong's government revised the implementing rules under the National Security Law to make it a criminal offense to refuse to hand over passwords or decryption assistance for personal electronic devices, phones and laptops included, when demanded by police. The rule applies to everyone present in Hong Kong, including tourists and passengers merely transiting the airport, no judicial warrant is required for the demand, and refusal carries up to six months in jail and a fine of up to HK$100,000. The US State Department, alongside several other governments, issued heightened travel guidance in response, and Hong Kong's existing advisory level sits at Level 2, exercise increased caution, largely because of arbitrary enforcement of local security laws.

On cost, Hong Kong remains flatly more expensive than mainland China across dining, hotels, and most day-to-day spending, though it rewards travelers who eat where locals eat. A cha chaan teng meal runs about HK$58 to HK$120, dim sum for one is HK$120 to HK$250, and fine dining starts around HK$1,500 per person before a mandatory 10 percent service charge kicks in at upscale spots. Hotels range from roughly HK$348 a night in hostels to HK$1,400-plus at the luxury end, with harbourfront rooms in Central commonly landing between HK$1,500 and HK$2,500 a night, and a reintroduced 3 percent hotel accommodation tax applies on top of the room rate. The Peak Tram, still the classic Victoria Peak run, now charges HK$82 one way or HK$116 return for adults after a fare increase that landed harder on children's and seniors' tickets, which rose nearly 40 percent to HK$52 one way and HK$75 return.
destinations.what_great:
The transit system is genuinely the best reason to visit. Octopus works across MTR, buses, ferries and most convenience stores with almost no friction, the Airport Express gets you into Central in about 24 minutes, and Hong Kong scrapped its arrival card entirely in October 2024 so getting through immigration is faster than it used to be. Since December 2025, transit passengers with at least seven hours between flights can even take a free guided airport tour along one of three themed routes with an English-speaking guide, which is a real way to turn a long layover into something useful.

The city also delivers a genuine high-low split that few places manage. You can eat extremely well at a cha chaan teng for the price of a fast food meal back home, then ride the Peak Tram up for a Victoria Harbour skyline view that costs nothing once you are up there, or splurge on Michelin-level dining a few blocks away. Visa-free access for most Western passports up to 90 days, and 180 days for UK citizens, means most travelers can plan a trip with zero visa paperwork.
destinations.what_ruined:
The single biggest problem with visiting Hong Kong right now is not price, it is the March 23, 2026 change to National Security Law enforcement rules. Police can now demand the password or decryption help for any personal device, phone or laptop, from anyone in the territory, including a tourist just transiting the airport, without a warrant, and refusing is a jailable offense. That is a real, current legal risk that did not exist a couple of years ago and it has pushed multiple governments, including the US, to sharpen their travel guidance.

Cost is the other honest friction point. Hong Kong is simply more expensive than mainland China for dining and lodging, hotel rooms near the harbour regularly run HK$1,500 to HK$2,500 a night before the reintroduced 3 percent hotel tax, and the Peak Tram just raised its fares again, hitting children's and seniors' tickets with an almost 40 percent jump. None of it is a scam, it is just a genuinely expensive city that charges accordingly.
tips: Buy the no-deposit Tourist Octopus for HK$39 if you do not want to deal with reclaiming the HK$50 deposit on the standard HK$150 On-Loan Octopus before you fly out.
Tap into the Airport Express with an Octopus card instead of buying a counter ticket, it drops the Hong Kong Station fare from HK$130 to HK$120.

Assume any device you carry can be searched: as of March 23, 2026 refusing to give police your phone or laptop password is a criminal offense with up to six months in jail, so travel with only what you are comfortable unlocking.
If you hold an Indian passport, complete the free Pre-Arrival Registration online before you fly, it is required in addition to the 14-day visa-free allowance and now covers applicants as young as 7.
Skip hotel restaurants for cha chaan teng diners, a full local meal runs about HK$58 to HK$120 versus HK$1,500-plus per person at fine dining spots.
Book Peak Tram tickets in advance if possible since 2026 fare increases pushed adult return tickets to HK$116 and child and senior tickets rose nearly 40 percent to HK$75 return.

guide.title: Hong Kong Practical Guide: Transit, Timing, and What Things Actually Cost in 2026
guide.summary: How to move around Hong Kong cheaply, when the weather and crowds actually cooperate, and where the real money goes.
guide.body:
Getting around is the easiest part of a Hong Kong trip. Buy an Octopus card the moment you land, either the standard HK$150 On-Loan version with its refundable HK$50 deposit or the no-deposit HK$39 Tourist Octopus, and use it on the MTR, buses, ferries, and most convenience stores for the rest of the trip. The Airport Express is the fastest way into town, reaching Hong Kong Station in around 24 minutes for HK$120 with Octopus, and from there the MTR network covers almost everything a visitor needs, with typical single fares landing between HK$3 and HK$30 depending on distance.

Timing matters more than most guides admit. Hong Kong's climate swings hard between a hot, humid, typhoon-prone summer and a cooler, drier autumn and early winter that most travelers find far more comfortable for walking the harbourfront or riding the Peak Tram. Autumn also tends to bring clearer skies for the Victoria Peak skyline views that are the city's signature free attraction once you have paid the tram fare up.

Neighborhood choice changes your budget more than almost anything else. Central and the harbourfront near Victoria Harbour deliver the postcard views but also the HK$1,500 to HK$2,500 nightly hotel rates, plus a 3 percent hotel accommodation tax that was reintroduced in 2025 and still applies. Staying slightly further out, in areas like Mong Kok or Sham Shui Po in Kowloon, cuts lodging costs sharply while keeping you a short, cheap MTR ride from everything, and it puts you closer to the cha chaan teng diners and dim sum spots where a full meal costs a fraction of what a hotel restaurant charges.

On paperwork, the process is genuinely lighter than it used to be. Hong Kong dropped its arrival card requirement entirely in October 2024, so most visitors from visa-free countries walk straight through immigration using only their passport and the airline's advance passenger information. The one real complication is the March 2026 change to device-search powers under the National Security Law, which now lets police demand phone or laptop passwords from anyone in the territory without a warrant, so treat your devices with the same caution you would in any jurisdiction with broad search authority, and keep sensitive data backed up elsewhere rather than carried on the device itself.

rating_rationale.overall: World-class transit, simplified entry, and a real high-low dining and sightseeing split make it a strong destination despite the friction.
rating_rationale.safety: Low street crime but US State Dept keeps Hong Kong at Level 2, and the March 2026 warrantless device-password law is a concrete new legal risk for visitors.
rating_rationale.value: Genuinely more expensive than mainland China on hotels and dining, though Octopus transit and street-level food keep a budget trip possible.

facts_checked: Standard On-Loan Octopus card costs HK$150 (HK$50 refundable deposit plus HK$100 starting balance); no-deposit Tourist Octopus costs HK$39
MTR single fares run roughly HK$3 to HK$30 depending on distance
Airport Express fares: HK$130 counter / HK$120 Octopus to Hong Kong Station; HK$115 / HK$105 to Kowloon Station; HK$80 / HK$73 to Tsing Yi
Hong Kong eliminated arrival/departure card requirements for all travelers on October 16, 2024, using airline Advance Passenger Information instead
Visa-free access covers roughly 170 countries; US/Canada/Australia/NZ/most EU up to 90 days, UK citizens up to 180 days
Indian passport holders get 14 days visa-free entry but must complete Pre-Arrival Registration (PAR); PAR minimum applicant age lowered from 11 to 7 effective January 19, 2026
Peak Tram adult fares as of 2026: HK$82 one way, HK$116 return; child/elderly fares HK$52 one way, HK$75 return after a fare increase (adult fares up 7-8%, child/elderly up nearly 40%)
US State Department travel advisory for Hong Kong is Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution, citing arbitrary enforcement of local laws including national security-related laws

On March 23, 2026, Hong Kong changed National Security Law implementing rules to make refusing to give police passwords/decryption assistance for personal electronic devices a criminal offense, applying to all travelers including transit passengers, with no judicial authorization required and penalties up to six months in jail and HK$100,000 fine
A 3% hotel accommodation tax was reintroduced in 2025 and remains in effect in 2026
Hotel price ranges: roughly HK$348/night hostels, HK$538/night 3-star, HK$1,400+/night luxury, HK$1,500-2,500/night in Central/Victoria Harbour
Dining price ranges: cha chaan teng meal roughly HK$58-120, dim sum HK$120-250 per person, fine dining from HK$1,500 per person, with a mandatory 10% service charge common at upscale restaurants

Hong Kong International Airport has offered complimentary guided tours for transit passengers with 7+ hour layovers since December 2025, featuring three 4-hour themed routes with English-speaking guides

destinations.name: Istanbul
destinations.summary: Istanbul delivers 2,500 years of layered history for a fraction of what a comparable European capital costs, but rapid lira inflation, aggressive taxi scams, and genuine earthquake risk mean the trip requires more homework than the postcards suggest.
destinations.headline: Istanbul in 2026: staggering history, rising prices, and scams you need to plan around before you land
destinations.body:
Istanbul is the only major city straddling two continents, and the density of world-class sights in a walkable radius, Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, Topkapi Palace, the Grand Bazaar, is hard to match anywhere. That said, the city has changed fast. Turkey's inflation has run above 30 percent through 2025, and hotel, restaurant, and attraction prices have climbed accordingly, with tourism industry data showing a roughly 5 percent drop in visitor arrivals in July 2025 as travelers balked at costs that now rival or exceed Greece and Spain.

The big sights are no longer casual walk-ins. Hagia Sophia has charged foreign visitors a separate entry fee since January 2024, currently 25 euros for access to the upper gallery museum area, payable in euros or lira, with children under 8 free. Topkapi Palace costs 2,750 Turkish lira at the gate for the combined Palace, Harem, and Hagia Irene ticket, roughly 55 euros, and closes on Tuesdays. The Blue Mosque, by contrast, remains free with no ticket required, but it is an active mosque that shuts to tourists roughly five times a day for prayer and stays closed until around 14:30 on Fridays for the main congregational prayer, so plan around the schedule rather than showing up whenever.

Getting into the city from the airport is where a lot of trips go sideways. Istanbul Airport (IST) taxi ranks have a documented pattern of complaints, meters that run long routes, invented toll charges, and drivers claiming the card machine is broken to force cash payment, with tourist reviews describing this behavior into 2025. Stick to the official taxi queue, insist the meter is running, or use the HAVAIST shuttle bus, about 275 lira one way and card-or-app only since HAVAIST stopped accepting cash. From Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) on the Asian side, the HAVABUS to Taksim runs about 440 lira in cash, with roughly a 100 lira surcharge if you pay by card, and takes about 90 minutes.

Getting around the city itself is cheap relative to Western Europe even after the price hikes. An Istanbulkart transit card costs 130 lira to buy, and a single ride on metro, tram, bus, or ferry starts at 27 lira, dropping to 19.33, then 14.67, then as low as 9.27 lira for additional transfers within the same trip window. Entry requirements depend heavily on nationality: EU, UK, Japanese, and several other passport holders currently enter visa-free for up to 90 days, while US, Canadian, Australian, and many other travelers need an e-Visa, obtainable only at the official evisa.gov.tr site for about 50 dollars, valid 180 days for a 90-day stay. Third-party sites that charge more for the same e-Visa are a real problem, so bookmark the official URL before you go.

Two background realities are worth knowing rather than ignoring. Turkey passed a controversial 2024 law requiring municipalities to remove stray dogs from the streets into shelters, and Istanbul's governor's office pushed a city-wide roundup deadline in 2025, so the free-roaming cats and dogs the city was famous for are visibly fewer and the topic is politically charged locally. Separately, Istanbul sits roughly 20 kilometers from the North Anatolian Fault, one of the world's most active fault lines; a magnitude 6.2 quake hit the Marmara Sea area in April 2025, and geoscientists have estimated as high as a 65 percent chance of a magnitude 7.0 or larger quake striking the region before 2030. It shouldn't cancel a trip, but it is worth knowing where your hotel's stairwells are.
destinations.what_great: The sheer concentration of history is unmatched, you can walk from a 6th-century Byzantine cathedral to a 17th-century Ottoman mosque to a 15th-century sultan's palace in under twenty minutes, all sitting on the same peninsula where Europe meets Asia. The food scene runs from three-lira simit carts to genuinely excellent seafood on the Bosphorus, and the ferry rides across the strait remain one of the great cheap thrills in world travel, all included on the same Istanbulkart you use for the metro.
destinations.what_ruined: The gap between what Istanbul used to cost and what it costs now catches a lot of travelers off guard, hotel and restaurant prices have risen over 40 percent year on year by some measures, and the major museums now charge foreign-visitor-only prices that can hit 55 euros a head. Layer on well-documented airport taxi scams targeting exactly the tourists who just landed and don't know the going rate, mosque visiting hours that don't accommodate a tight itinerary, and background anxiety about a fault line the city sits directly on top of, and the trip demands more logistics planning than its reputation as an easy long weekend suggests.
tips: Buy an Istanbulkart (130 lira for the card) rather than paying cash fares; a single ride starts at 27 lira and each transfer within the window drops to 19.33, then 14.67, then as low as 9.27 lira.
Hagia Sophia charges foreign visitors 25 euros for the upper gallery area, a fee in place since January 2024; children under 8 enter free with ID.
Topkapi Palace's combined Palace, Harem, and Hagia Irene ticket runs 2,750 lira (about 55 euros) at the gate; it's closed Tuesdays and last entry is 16:30.

The Blue Mosque is free with no ticket needed, but it closes to visitors roughly five times a day for prayer and until about 14:30 on Fridays, and dress code (shoulders and knees covered, headscarf for women) is enforced, so bring your own scarf rather than relying on the communal ones at the door.

From Istanbul Airport (IST), the HAVAIST shuttle bus runs about 275 lira one way and is card or app only, cash is no longer accepted; from Sabiha Gökçen (SAW), HAVABUS to Taksim is about 440 lira cash (roughly 100 lira more by card) and takes about 90 minutes.

Only take taxis from the official marked ranks, confirm the meter is running before you move, and use an app like BiTaksi to lock in the route; a common airport scam is a driver claiming the card machine is broken to force a cash payment at an inflated rate.

Check your visa status before booking: US, Canadian, and Australian citizens (among others) need an e-Visa, about 50 dollars, only through the official evisa.gov.tr site, while EU, UK, and Japanese passport holders currently enter visa-free for 90 days.

Visit March to May or September to November for the best mix of mild weather and manageable crowds; August is the hottest and busiest month, while December through February is the cheapest but brings cold, rain, and occasional snow.

guide.title: Istanbul travel guide 2026: airports, transit, neighborhoods, and mosque rules explained
guide.summary: A practical rundown of how to actually move through Istanbul in 2026, from choosing the right airport transfer to picking a base neighborhood to not offending anyone at the mosque.
guide.body:
Istanbul has two airports and picking the wrong one changes your day. Istanbul Airport (IST) on the European side is the main international hub and where most long-haul flights land; the HAVAIST shuttle bus network connects it to the city for about 275 lira one way, card or app only since cash was phased out, though there's no longer a direct HAVAIST line straight into Sultanahmet, you connect via the HVL-1 route to Beyazıt-Aksaray and pick up the T1 tram. Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) on the Asian side handles a large share of budget and regional carriers; the HAVABUS to Taksim costs about 440 lira in cash (card payment adds roughly a 100 lira surcharge) and takes about 90 minutes, so factor that into any tight connection.

Once you're in the city, buy an Istanbulkart immediately, it's 130 lira for the card and covers metro, tram, bus, and ferry, with the first ride at 27 lira and each transfer within the transfer window getting progressively cheaper, down to about 9.27 lira. The ferries in particular are worth using for their own sake, not just as transport, the crossing between the European and Asian sides past the Bosphorus waterfront is one of the best cheap experiences the city offers and it's covered by the same card as the bus.

Where you stay matters more here than in most cities because the historic peninsula, modern nightlife district, and Asian-side neighborhoods each offer a genuinely different trip. Sultanahmet puts you within walking distance of Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, and Topkapi Palace, which is convenient for a first visit but means tour groups and touts outside your hotel door from morning to night. Beyoğlu and Karaköy, across the Golden Horn, put you closer to the restaurant and nightlife scene along Istiklal Street and the waterfront, with a livelier but louder base. Kadıköy, on the Asian side, is quieter, more residential, and popular with travelers who want a local feel and don't mind a ferry ride to reach the major sights.

Mosque etiquette is not optional and gets enforced at the door. At the Blue Mosque and other active mosques, women need their hair, neck, and shoulders covered and legs covered to below the knee, and men need to avoid shorts above the knee; shoes come off before entering. Free scarves and wraps are available at the entrance but they're shared and not always clean, so bringing a lightweight scarf and covering layer of your own is more comfortable. Remember mosques close to visitors around five times a day for prayer, with Fridays closed until roughly 14:30, so check timing before you build it into a tight itinerary.

On money, card acceptance is widespread in restaurants, shops, and hotels, but carrying some lira in cash is still useful for the HAVABUS, small vendors, and situations where a driver or shop claims their card machine is down, a known tactic worth being skeptical of rather than an automatic reason to hand over cash. With inflation running high, prices you see quoted in older blog posts or guidebooks are likely to be understated, budget with a buffer rather than trusting a number that's more than a few months old.

rating_rationale.overall: The historical density and food scene genuinely earn a high score, but the friction of scam-prone transport and unpredictable pricing keeps it just below the top tier.
rating_rationale.safety: Violent crime against tourists is low and the city is walkable, but airport taxi scams are well documented into 2025, and the region carries a scientifically estimated elevated earthquake risk that residents and officials both take seriously.
rating_rationale.value: Transit and street food remain genuinely cheap, but sustained 30-plus percent inflation has pushed hotel, restaurant, and major-museum prices to levels that now rival Western Europe, eroding the value Istanbul used to be known for.

destinations.name: Kyoto
destinations.summary: Japan's former imperial capital, dense with UNESCO temples and machiya streets, now managing record crowds with new taxes, fines and visitor-priced buses.
destinations.headline: Kyoto in 2026: World-Class Heritage, Priced and Policed Like Never Before
destinations.body:
Kyoto rewards travelers who plan around its pressure points rather than walking straight into them. The city is the heart of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage listing, which also reaches into Uji and Otsu, and drew 10.88 million foreign visitors in 2024, and the strain now shows up in policy. From March 1, 2026 the municipal lodging tax runs on five tiers charged per person, per night: 200 yen for rooms under 6,000 yen, 400 yen from 6,000 to 19,999 yen, 1,000 yen from 20,000 to 49,999 yen, 4,000 yen from 50,000 to 99,999 yen, and 10,000 yen at 100,000 yen and above. That top band is the steepest lodging tax in Japan, and it applies to every guest in the room, not to the room itself.

The geography is simple once you accept it. The eastern strip, Higashiyama, carries the postcard sites: Kiyomizu-dera at 500 yen for adults, Ginkakuji, Nanzen-ji and the Gion entertainment district. The northwest holds Kinkaku-ji, also 500 yen, open 9:00 to 17:00. Central Kyoto has Nijo Castle at 800 yen for the grounds or 1,300 yen including Ninomaru Palace, with Honmaru Palace sold as a separate 1,000 yen ticket that requires advance reservation. South of the station, Fushimi Inari Taisha and its torii corridors are free and open around the clock, which is exactly why the lower paths fill before nine in the morning.

Gion now carries enforcement, not just etiquette signage. The narrow lanes off Hanamikoji Street are private property, and the local residents' council posts a 10,000 yen penalty for entering them, introduced after repeated incidents of visitors harassing geiko and maiko and intruding on residents. Hanamikoji Street itself remains public. The main street itself remains public, and patrols have been expanded to steer people back onto it.

Transport is the daily friction point. City buses run a 230 yen flat fare inside the central zone, but the old 700 yen bus-only day pass was scrapped deliberately, to push visitors off the routes locals commute on. The replacement is the Subway and Bus 1-Day Pass at 1,100 yen for adults and 550 yen for children. Kyoto also runs the EX100 and EX101 sightseeing limited express buses at 500 yen a ride, priced above the standard fare on purpose, reaching Gojozaka for Kiyomizu-dera in roughly ten minutes from Kyoto Station, Gion in seventeen and Ginkakuji in thirty. The city has signalled a resident-priority fare structure, around 200 yen for residents against 350 to 400 yen for everyone else, targeted for rollout by fiscal 2027.

Seasonality is not a preference here, it is the entire trip. Cherry blossoms peak from late March into the first days of April. The tsuyu rainy season runs early June to mid-July. July and August deliver highs above 33C with humidity over 70 percent, and July is also Gion Matsuri month, stacking festival crowds on top of the heat. Autumn foliage peaks from mid-November into early December. Those two colour windows produce the year's highest room rates, and Kyoto sits among the most expensive major Japanese cities for a hotel room over Golden Week.

An honest visitor should expect a city that is genuinely extraordinary and genuinely oversubscribed at the same time. Temples close earlier than most people assume, commonly around 17:00. Many smaller temples and shrine offices still want cash in yen and will not take a card. Kyoto publishes an official hourly congestion forecast covering Gion, Arashiyama and the Kiyomizu approach, and it is worth reading before leaving the hotel. Travelers who start at 6:30am, favour subway and rail over buses, and space the famous sites across separate mornings get a completely different city from the one experienced by people queueing at eleven.
destinations.what_great: The concentration is unmatched, seventeen UNESCO component sites inside one mid-sized city, with Fushimi Inari free and open at all hours and both Kinkaku-ji and Kiyomizu-dera at just 500 yen for adults. Transit is punctual, and ICOCA, Suica and PASMO IC cards all work on city buses and the subway. Food value stays strong even with a weak yen, with excellent ramen and set lunches well under 2,000 yen. Late-March blossom and mid-November foliage are legitimately world-class.
destinations.what_ruined: Kyoto is now openly rationing visitors. The lodging tax moved to five tiers on March 1, 2026, topping out at 10,000 yen per person per night. The bus-only day pass was abolished to keep tourists off local routes, and tourist-priced express buses cost 500 yen against the 230 yen flat fare. Gion's private alleys carry a 10,000 yen trespass fine. Arashiyama's bamboo grove and the Kiyomizu approach are shoulder to shoulder by mid-morning, and peak-season rooms hit record rates.
tips: Buy the HARUKA one-way discount ticket from Kansai Airport to Kyoto Station at 2,200 yen for adults and 1,100 yen for children, which requires a foreign passport and Temporary Visitor status.

The EX100 and EX101 sightseeing express buses cost 500 yen in cash but run on limited days and are included at no additional fare in the 1,100 yen Subway and Bus 1-Day Pass, so pass holders should use them rather than avoid them.
Reach Fushimi Inari Taisha before 8:00am, because it charges nothing and never closes, so the upper torii paths are effectively empty at dawn.
Budget 1,300 yen for Nijo Castle including Ninomaru Palace, and reserve the separate 1,000 yen Honmaru Palace ticket in advance if you want to see it.
Do not step into the private alleys off Hanamikoji Street in Gion, where the residents' council posts a 10,000 yen penalty for entering.
Check Kyoto's official hourly congestion forecast at global.kyoto.travel before committing a morning to Arashiyama or the Kiyomizu approach.

guide.title: Kyoto Trip Planner 2026: Costs, Crowds, Transit and the New Lodging Tax
guide.summary: A month-by-month, fare-by-fare planning guide to Kyoto in 2026, covering airport transfers, the restructured lodging tax, temple entry fees, realistic daily budgets and where the crowds actually sit.
guide.body:
January and February are the cheapest and emptiest months in Kyoto, cold but comparatively dry, with business hotel rates falling well below spring levels. March warms fast, and cherry blossoms usually peak from late March into the first days of April, which is the single most crowded and most expensive window of the year alongside November. Late April and early May bring Golden Week, when Kyoto room rates run among the highest in the country and availability collapses. The tsuyu rainy season settles in from early June to mid-July. July and August are punishing, with highs above 33C and humidity over 70 percent, and July is also Gion Matsuri month. September carries typhoon risk, with Kyoto typically catching one to three storms in the late-August to September stretch. October is the quiet compromise nobody talks about. Autumn foliage peaks from mid-November into early December, spectacular and completely mobbed.

Kansai International is the main gateway, roughly 75 to 90 minutes from Kyoto. The JR HARUKA limited express runs direct to Kyoto Station, and foreign passport holders entering Japan on Temporary Visitor status can buy a discounted one-way HARUKA ticket for 2,200 yen for adults and 1,100 yen for children, materially cheaper than paying the standard base fare plus limited express charge. Buy it before clearing the JR gates and carry your passport, since it must be presented at purchase. Limousine buses also run from both Kansai and Osaka Itami. Taxis from Kansai are extremely expensive and only make sense for a group arriving after the last train, which departs Kansai for Kyoto around 10:16pm.

Kyoto is a rail city pretending to be a bus city. City buses charge a 230 yen flat fare in the central zone and are the single most congested part of the network, which is why the old 700 yen bus-only day pass was deliberately abolished. The Subway and Bus 1-Day Pass at 1,100 yen for adults and 550 yen for children covers both municipal subway lines, most city bus routes, and the EX100 and EX101 sightseeing express buses that otherwise cost 500 yen per ride. ICOCA, Suica and PASMO cards work across buses and subway. Rented bicycles are genuinely the fastest way across the flat central grid, and walking Higashiyama end to end beats queueing at Kyoto Station bus stop D, which regularly fills to capacity and leaves people waiting for the next bus.

Fushimi Inari Taisha is free, open at all hours, and the only major site you can realistically have to yourself if you arrive by 8:00am; walk past the first dense torii tunnel and the crowd thins dramatically. Kinkaku-ji costs 500 yen and is open 9:00 to 17:00, and it is a single fixed viewing loop of maybe twenty-five minutes, so treat it as a stop rather than a morning. Kiyomizu-dera is 500 yen, and the approach streets of Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka are both the real attraction and the real crush. Nijo Castle is 800 yen for the grounds or 1,300 yen with Ninomaru Palace and its nightingale floors, with Honmaru Palace a separate 1,000 yen reserved ticket and the painting gallery another 100 yen. Arashiyama's bamboo grove is free and, honestly, close to a skip after 9:00am, since it is a short path; nearby Tenryu-ji and the wider Sagano area repay the trip far better. Gion is worth an evening on Hanamikoji Street itself, never in the side alleys.

Budget roughly 130 to 200 USD per person for a mid-range day in Kyoto in 2026. Budget accommodation in a business hotel typically sits around 60 to 110 USD in shoulder season and considerably more in April and November, with reported peak-season business hotel rates climbing from about 10,000 yen to 25,000 yen a night, plus the per-person lodging tax of 200 to 1,000 yen at those price points. Food is the bargain of the trip, with ramen or a set lunch around 6 to 10 USD and a good dinner 20 to 35 USD. Transit costs about 8 USD a day with the 1,100 yen pass. Temple entries run 3 to 9 USD each, and three a day is plenty. Backpackers can hold 70 to 90 USD a day with hostels and convenience store meals. Anyone booking a ryokan with kaiseki should expect 300 USD and up, and the top lodging tax band of 10,000 yen per person per night applies once the nightly rate reaches 100,000 yen.

Kyoto is one of the safest large cities anywhere and violent crime against visitors is rare, so the risks are procedural rather than personal. Carry cash, because smaller temples, shrine offices and older restaurants still refuse cards, and IC card top-ups need yen. Avoid unlicensed geisha-experience touts, and never photograph geiko or maiko without explicit consent, which Gion now enforces, alongside the residents' council's 10,000 yen penalty for entering the private alleys off Hanamikoji. Expect luggage friction on crowded buses at peak times. Above all, check the city's official congestion forecast before setting out, since it is published specifically because the crowd problem is real.

destinations.name: Lima
destinations.summary: World-class food capital in a genuinely two-tier city: Miraflores and Barranco feel like Latin America's safest streets, while the historic center turns risky after dark.
destinations.headline: Lima has the world's best restaurant and a curfew problem: the honest split-city guide
destinations.body:
Lima earned its current bragging rights the hard way. In June 2025, Maido, chef Mitsuharu Tsumura's Nikkei restaurant in Miraflores, was named the World's Best Restaurant by the World's 50 Best Restaurants list, with Kjolle, Pia Leon's restaurant, landing at number 9 the same year. Maido runs a single tasting menu, the Maido Experience, ten-plus courses with no a la carte option, starting around S/1,295 per person (roughly $331) before any wine pairing, with pairings running S/1,985 to S/2,525. Central, Virgilio Martinez's altitude-themed tasting menu restaurant, sits nearby in the same price bracket, with its Mundo en Desnivel and Alturas Mater Vegetal menus running about PEN 1,600 to 1,630 per person (roughly $420 to $440) before pairings, and reservations get genuinely hard to land during the June through September high season, so booking months out matters more than it does almost anywhere else in South America.

That is the postcard version. The honest version is that Lima is a split city, and treating it as one neighborhood will get you either bored or robbed. Miraflores and Barranco, the coastal districts where most visitors actually stay and eat, are comfortable to walk by day and generally fine on well-lit streets at night, Barranco's nightlife strip included, provided you keep phones out of reach of scooters and use a rideshare between far-apart bars. Lima's historic center, Lima Centro, with its colonial plazas and UNESCO-listed architecture, is a legitimate daytime sightseeing draw and a place most guides and locals tell you to leave before dark. The U.S. State Department has Peru at Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution, as of May 2025, with a Crime C indicator flagging widespread violent and organized crime and limited police capacity in places, and it separately assesses Lima as a high-threat location for crime affecting official U.S. interests, though crime in Lima reportedly fell about 11.1 percent from January to July 2025.

Getting in got easier in 2025: Jorge Chavez International's new $2.4 billion terminal opened June 1, 2025, roughly three times the size of the old one, with 46 gates versus 19 previously and a second runway operating since April 2023. Getting from that airport into the city is where the friction starts. Official airport taxi desks in arrivals quote fixed fares, typically S/60 to 95 to Miraflores depending on time of day, and that premium buys real safety: unofficial touts outside the terminal doors have been linked to express kidnappings where passengers are driven to ATMs, so skipping the counter to save a few soles is not a smart trade. Inside the city, Uber, Cabify, and InDriver are the safer default over hailing a taxi off the street; InDriver works differently in that you propose a fare and drivers accept, decline, or counter it rather than getting a fixed quote upfront. Money-wise, the sol has been stable through mid-2026, trading around 3.39 to 3.40 soles per dollar, and Lima remains one of the cheaper big Latin American capitals to eat in day to day: a menu del dia set lunch, soup, a main like lomo saltado, and a drink, runs about 12 to 15 soles, around $3 to $4, in tourist-adjacent areas and closer to 9 or 10 soles in local neighborhoods, a gap of literally hundreds of dollars per person from a Central tasting menu at the same latitude.
destinations.what_great:
The food scene is not hype. Maido holding the World's Best Restaurant title as of the 2025 World's 50 Best list, with Central and Kjolle also in the global top ten, means Lima has more legitimate claim to being a world food capital right now than almost any city outside Europe or Japan, and that quality cascades down into a huge, genuinely cheap ceviche and anticucho scene that has nothing to do with the tasting menus. Miraflores and Barranco are walkable, ocean-adjacent, dense with cafes and street art, and rated among the safest areas in Latin America to be a pedestrian, day or night on the main streets. The new Jorge Chavez terminal is a real upgrade too: more gates, more capacity, and an easier arrivals experience than the cramped old terminal.

Entry logistics are also low-friction for U.S. travelers: no visa required for tourist stays up to 90 days, sometimes extendable to 183 at the immigration officer's discretion, and a stable, favorable exchange rate around 3.4 soles to the dollar makes budgeting easy and stretches everyday spending a long way outside the fine-dining bracket.
destinations.what_ruined:
The safety picture is not uniform, and pretending it is would be dishonest. Lima Centro, the historic downtown with the plazas and colonial churches everyone wants to photograph, is described consistently as unsafe after dark, and the State Department's Level 2 advisory for Peru flags widespread crime and a high-threat designation specifically for Lima. Unofficial street taxis are the sharpest edge of that risk: no meter, no company markings, and a documented pattern of express kidnappings where tourists are driven to ATMs and forced to withdraw cash, which is exactly why every credible source says to use the official counter in arrivals or an app, never a tout at the curb.

Then there is the price gap at the top of the food scene, which is real friction if you came for the world's-best-restaurant headline: Central and Maido both run well past $300 to $400 per person before wine, reservations at Central are tight enough in high season that casual walk-in hopes are unrealistic, and neither restaurant does a la carte, so there is no cheaper way in. Budget for it as a splurge, not a meal.
tips: Book Central or Maido at least 2 to 3 months ahead if traveling June through September; Central's tasting menus run about PEN 1,600 to 1,630 (roughly $420 to $440) and Maido's start near S/1,295 (about $331), both before wine pairings, and neither offers a la carte.

At Jorge Chavez airport, go to the official taxi desk inside arrivals rather than accepting offers at the curb; fixed fares to Miraflores run roughly S/60 to 95 depending on time of day, and unofficial touts have been linked to express-kidnapping scams.
Use Uber, Cabify, or InDriver over street-hailed taxis once in the city; note InDriver has you propose a fare that drivers can accept or counter, rather than a fixed upfront price like Uber.

Plan to leave Lima Centro (the historic downtown) before dark; it is a legitimate daytime sightseeing stop but is widely and consistently flagged as unsafe at night, unlike Miraflores and Barranco's main streets.

Carry passports valid at least 6 months past your entry date; U.S. citizens get visa-free tourist entry up to 90 days (occasionally extendable to 183 at the immigration officer's discretion) via the TAM card issued on arrival.

For everyday food, a menu del dia set lunch, soup, a main course, a drink, runs about 12 to 15 soles (roughly $3 to $4) in tourist-friendlier areas, and can drop to 9 or 10 soles in local neighborhoods, a useful budget baseline against the city's headline tasting menus.

guide.title: Lima Travel Guide: Getting Around the Split City
guide.summary: A practical guide to moving through Lima's safer coastal districts, timing the historic center right, and stretching a favorable exchange rate.
guide.body:
Base yourself in Miraflores or Barranco rather than downtown. Both districts sit along the Costa Verde coastline, are walkable, and are rated among the safest areas in Lima and in Latin America generally for pedestrians, with Barranco carrying more nightlife and Miraflores more of the parks, malls, and business-traveler infrastructure. Lima Centro, the colonial historic core with its cathedral and government palace, is worth a focused daytime visit but is not where most guides recommend staying, and locals and travel advisories alike are consistent that it should be left before evening.

Getting from Jorge Chavez airport into the city changed in 2025 with the opening of a new $2.4 billion terminal on June 1, roughly three times the size of the old one with 46 gates instead of 19. From arrivals, go straight to the official taxi counter rather than engaging anyone offering rides outside the doors; expect a fixed fare in the S/60 to 95 range to Miraflores depending on time of day and traffic. Inside the city, Uber, Cabify, and InDriver cover most trips reliably; InDriver's negotiated-fare model is different enough from a standard app that first-time users should expect to counter-offer rather than get an instant fixed price.

On money, the sol has held fairly steady through the first half of 2026 around 3.39 to 3.40 to the dollar, and daily costs stay low outside the tasting-menu tier: budget roughly 6 to 10 soles for a simple breakfast, 12 to 15 soles for a menu del dia lunch with soup, a main, and a drink, and 15 to 20 soles for a simple dinner. That means a traveler can eat extremely well on a modest daily budget and then deliberately splurge once on a Central or Maido reservation without either extreme distorting the trip's overall cost. High season for both dining reservations and general crowding runs June through September, so book restaurant tables and, if relevant, any Machu Picchu connections well in advance for that window. U.S. citizens do not need a visa for tourist stays up to 90 days, receive a TAM entry card at the border or airport, and should carry a passport valid at least six months beyond the entry date to avoid being turned away.

rating_rationale.overall: World-class, currently-ranked-number-one dining plus a walkable, likeable coastal core, offset by a genuine after-dark safety split that demands planning.
rating_rationale.safety: Miraflores and Barranco are comparatively very safe by day and night on lit streets; Lima Centro at night and unofficial street taxis carry documented, specific risks including express kidnapping.
rating_rationale.value: Everyday costs, menu del dia lunches, transit, casual meals, are genuinely cheap at a roughly 3.4 sol to dollar rate, while the headline tasting menus sit at true international luxury pricing.

facts_checked: Maido was named The World's Best Restaurant on the 2025 World's 50 Best Restaurants list (announced June 2025); Kjolle ranked number 9 the same year.
Maido's Maido Experience tasting menu starts around S/1,295 per person (about $331) without wine pairing; pairings run S/1,985 to S/2,525.
Central's tasting menus (Mundo en Desnivel / Alturas Mater Vegetal) run approximately PEN 1,600 to 1,630 per person (roughly $420 to $440) before pairings; pairings run about $95 to $180 separately.
Central operates lunch service 12:45 to 13:30 and dinner 19:00 to 20:30, Monday through Saturday.

Jorge Chavez International Airport's new terminal opened June 1, 2025, a $2.4 billion project roughly three times the size of the old terminal, with 46 gates versus 19 previously and a second runway operating since April 2023.
Official airport taxi fares from Jorge Chavez to Miraflores run approximately S/60 to 95 depending on time of day.

The U.S. State Department rated Peru at Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution, as of May 16, 2025, with a Crime 'C' indicator, and separately assesses Lima as a high-threat location for crime affecting U.S. government interests.
Crime in Lima declined approximately 11.1 percent from January to July 2025 according to State Department reporting.

Lima's historic center (Lima Centro) is widely described as safe for daytime sightseeing but unsafe at night, in contrast to Miraflores, Barranco, and San Isidro, which are described as generally safe to walk even at night on main streets.

Unofficial/unlicensed street taxis in Lima have been linked to express-kidnapping scams where passengers are taken to ATMs; official airport taxi desks and apps (Uber, Cabify, InDriver) are recommended alternatives.
InDriver uses a negotiated-fare model (riders propose a price drivers can accept, decline, or counter), unlike the fixed upfront pricing of Uber and Cabify.
As of early August 2026, the mid-market USD to PEN exchange rate is approximately 1 USD = 3.39 to 3.40 soles.

U.S. citizens do not need a visa for Peru tourist stays up to 90 days (occasionally extendable up to 183 days at immigration officer discretion), and receive a TAM entry card on arrival; passports must be valid at least 6 months from the entry date.
A menu del dia set lunch in Lima typically costs 12 to 15 soles (about $3.15 to $3.95), sometimes as low as 9 to 10 soles in non-touristy neighborhoods; a simple dinner runs about 15 to 20 soles.

destinations.name: Lisbon
destinations.summary: Portugal's Atlantic capital, hilly and tiled, still good value in Western Europe, now under short-term rental caps, tuk-tuk bans and heavy pickpocket pressure.
destinations.headline: Lisbon in 2026: Still Excellent Value, Now Openly Fighting Its Own Tourism
destinations.body:
Lisbon rewards travelers who accept that the city is having an argument with tourism in public. Portugal's capital is built across seven hills above the Tagus, and the sightseeing map is small: Baixa, the flat grid rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake, Alfama, the Moorish-era lane network below Castelo de Sao Jorge, Bairro Alto and Principe Real on the ridge above, and Belem, a few kilometres west, where the monuments are.

Costs remain moderate by Western European standards, but they are moving. The municipal tourist tax is 4 euros per person per night for guests aged 13 and over, capped at seven nights per stay. Transport fares rose on 1 January 2026: a single Carris or Metro journey on a navegante card is 1.90 euros, zapping pay-as-you-go is 1.72 euros, and the reusable navegante occasional card itself costs 0.50 euros. The 24-hour Carris and Metro ticket is 7.25 euros, rising to 10.35 euros including Transtejo ferries and 11.40 euros including CP trains, which is the version you want for Sintra or Cascais. Buying onboard is punished: 2.30 euros on a bus, 3.30 euros on a tram, 4.30 euros for a funicular such as the Gloria or the Bica, and 6.20 euros for the Santa Justa Lift.

The headline sites are straightforward. Castelo de Sao Jorge charges 17 euros for adults, 8.50 euros for ages 13 to 25, 14 euros for over-65s, 12 euros for visitors with specific needs, and is free for under-12s. In Belem, the Jeronimos Monastery cloister is ticketed while the adjoining church of Santa Maria de Belem is free to enter. The Torre de Belem reopened on 26 May 2026 after roughly a year of restoration and now runs strict timed entry, capped at 60 visitors every 30 minutes and 900 a day, Tuesday to Sunday, 09:30 to 17:30 with last entry at 17:00. That cap is a genuine constraint rather than a formality, and walk-up availability in summer is unlikely.

The overtourism response here is aimed at housing and streets rather than purely at your wallet. Lisbon's short-term rental containment rules, approved on 27 November 2025 and effective from 6 December 2025, block new Alojamento Local registrations in any parish where AL units already make up 10 percent or more of permanent housing, with an intermediate authorisation regime between 5 and 10 percent. That covers most of the historic centre, including Alfama, Baixa, Bairro Alto and Principe Real, and short-term rentals now account for roughly two thirds of Lisbon's tourist accommodation supply citywide. Tuk-tuks have been banned from 337 streets since April 2025, with EMEL fielding a dedicated inspection brigade alongside the municipal police. Housing marches moved through Lisbon in March 2026 under slogans tying tourism, aviation and rents together. Visitors are not the target, but they are unmistakably the subject.

Weather is the quiet advantage. Lisbon is comfortable across a far longer season than most European capitals, with mild wet winters and dry hot summers. July and August are the busiest and hottest stretch, and the shoulder months on either side are better in almost every respect.

An honest visitor should expect steep gradients and slick calcada paving that punishes bad shoes, and should expect the crowds to concentrate hard on three things: tram 28E, the Belem monuments, and the Alfama viewpoints at sunset. Everything else is comparatively calm. Restaurants outside the tourist grid remain good value, and the couvert of bread, olives and cheese placed on your table is chargeable rather than free, and can be sent back untouched.
destinations.what_great: Lisbon delivers unusually high quality for the money, with a compact core walkable in a day and genuinely good food a street or two off the tourist grid. Transit is cheap and integrated, 1.90 euros a journey on a navegante card and 7.25 euros for 24 hours across Carris and Metro. The Atlantic light and the Tagus viewpoints are exceptional. Belem's monuments are UNESCO-listed, and the restored Torre de Belem reopened in May 2026. Winters are mild enough to visit year-round.
destinations.what_ruined: Tram 28E is the worst pickpocket spot most Lisbon visitors will meet, and the Baixa and Rossio grid runs thick with fake-drug approaches used purely as cover for lifting wallets, the product usually being crushed leaves rather than anything illegal. Belem Tower is capped at 900 visitors a day, so unplanned visits simply fail. Onboard fares are punitive, 3.30 euros on a tram against 1.90 on a card. Rental caps and a 337-street tuk-tuk ban reflect real local anger.
tips: Buy the reusable navegante occasional card for 0.50 euros at any Metro machine and load zapping at 1.72 euros a journey instead of paying 3.30 euros onboard a tram.
Take the Metro Red Line from Humberto Delgado Airport for 1.90 euros rather than a taxi, which costs several times more.
Book a Torre de Belem timed slot ahead of arrival, because entry is capped at 60 people per 30 minutes and 900 per day, Tuesday to Sunday, with last entry at 17:00.
Ride tram 12E or a parallel bus rather than 28E, which is where most visitors who get pickpocketed in Lisbon get pickpocketed.
Budget 17 euros for adult entry to Castelo de Sao Jorge, and buy only through the castle's authorised BOL ticketing page or the on-site ticket office.
Decline the couvert of bread and olives if you do not want it, since it is charged to the bill, and expect the 4 euro per person nightly tourist tax at checkout.

guide.title: Lisbon Planning Guide 2026: Fares, Timed Entry, Real Budgets and Scam Hotspots
guide.summary: How to plan Lisbon in 2026: month-by-month timing, airport transfers, the January fare rise, which monuments now need booking, honest daily budgets, and where pickpockets actually work.
guide.body:
Lisbon has one of the longest usable seasons of any Western European capital, which means the month you choose changes cost far more than it changes comfort. March through early June is the sweet spot, warm and dry enough for the hills without August heat, and mid-September through October repeats it with warmer ocean water. July and August are the hottest and by far the most crowded, with cruise arrivals stacking on top of the summer flow, and this is when Belem and tram 28E become genuinely unpleasant. June brings the Santo Antonio street festivities that fill Alfama and Graca with grilled sardines and improvised bars. November through February is wet but mild, and the cheapest time to be here by a wide margin, with the caveat that hill streets get slick in rain.

Humberto Delgado Airport sits inside the city, roughly 20 to 30 minutes from the centre. The Metro Red Line runs directly from the terminal for 1.90 euros on a navegante card, or 1.72 euros with zapping, with the reusable card itself costing 0.50 euros. The old Aerobus was permanently discontinued in 2022, so ignore any guide still listing it. A metered taxi to central Lisbon is a modest fare rather than a rip-off, but Portugal's national taxi tariff was rewritten in 2026 onto a combined distance and time meter and meters were still being reprogrammed through the summer, so check the tariff card posted in the car before you set off. Never accept a ride from anyone who approaches you inside the terminal building, since those drivers are unregulated and charge whatever they like.

Getting around is cheap if you buy correctly and expensive if you do not. Load the navegante card and every Metro, Carris bus and tram journey costs 1.90 euros, or 1.72 with zapping. Pay the driver instead and a bus is 2.30 euros and a tram 3.30 euros. The 24-hour Carris and Metro ticket is 7.25 euros, the version including Transtejo ferries to Cacilhas is 10.35 euros, and the version including CP trains, which is what covers Sintra and Cascais, is 11.40 euros. The funiculars, Gloria, Bica and Lavra, are 4.30 euros for up to two journeys, and the Santa Justa Lift is 6.20 euros, which is poor value against the queue it usually carries. Walking is the default in the centre, but the gradients are real and the polished calcada stone is slippery in rain.

Castelo de Sao Jorge is the classic first stop at 17 euros for adults, 8.50 euros for ages 13 to 25, 14 euros for over-65s and free under 12, with the caveat that its main product is a view you can get free from Miradouro da Senhora do Monte or Miradouro da Graca. In Belem, the Jeronimos Monastery cloister is the genuinely unmissable interior in the city, and the adjacent church of Santa Maria de Belem is free. The Torre de Belem reopened on 26 May 2026 after a roughly one million euro restoration and now runs timed entry capped at 60 visitors per 30 minutes and 900 per day, Tuesday to Sunday 09:30 to 17:30 with last entry at 17:00, bookable online or at the Jeronimos ticket office; without a slot, do not plan on getting in. Alfama itself is the free attraction, best walked downhill from the castle in the early morning before the tour groups. Sintra, forty minutes by CP train, deserves a full day rather than an afternoon, and its palaces are ticketed separately from anything in Lisbon.

A realistic mid-range day in Lisbon in 2026 lands around 110 to 170 USD per person. Accommodation is the swing factor, with mid-range hotels typically 90 to 160 USD in shoulder season and higher in summer, plus the 4 euro per person nightly tourist tax for anyone 13 or over, capped at seven nights. Transit is 7.25 euros for a 24-hour Carris and Metro pass or roughly 4 to 6 euros a day on pay-as-you-go. Attractions run 8 to 20 euros each, with the 17 euro castle at the top of the normal range, so two paid sites a day is a sensible ceiling. Food is where Lisbon still wins, with coffee and pastries costing a couple of euros and a neighbourhood lunch a fraction of what the same meal costs in Paris or Amsterdam. Budget travellers can hold 55 to 80 USD a day using hostels, set lunches and the pass.

On safety, Lisbon ranks among Europe's safest capitals for violent crime, and the risk you actually face is theft. Tram 28E is the highest-risk single location in the city, worked by teams who block doors and create distractions in the crush; take 12E or a parallel bus instead, or ride 28E at 7am from the Martim Moniz terminus with your bag in front of you. Rossio and the Baixa grid are the second hotspot, where strangers offering drugs are almost never selling drugs, since the product is typically crushed leaves and the transaction is a pretext for a second person to lift your phone. Petition clipboards and shell games work the same squares. Keep nothing in a back pocket, use a zipped cross-body bag, and treat any unsolicited approach in Baixa as the opening move of a theft rather than a conversation.

rating_rationale.overall: A compact, walkable capital with UNESCO monuments in Belem, exceptional viewpoints and a long usable season, held back only by how concentrated the crowding has become.
rating_rationale.safety: Violent crime is low by European capital standards, but tram 28E is documented as the most pickpocketed transit line in Portugal and the Baixa and Rossio grid is a scam hotspot.
rating_rationale.value: Transit is cheap at 1.90 euros a journey and 7.25 euros for 24 hours, and food outside the tourist grid is strong value, though the 4 euro nightly tourist tax and 17 euro castle entry are creeping upward.

destinations.name: Marrakech
destinations.summary: Historic imperial city in central Morocco built around a walled UNESCO medina, the Jemaa el-Fna square, palace museums and the modern Gueliz district.
destinations.headline: Marrakech Delivers World-Class Monuments For 100 Dirhams, And Constant Hassle For Free
destinations.body:
Marrakech sits inland at the foot of the High Atlas, and almost everything visitors come for is packed inside the ochre walls of the medina, a UNESCO World Heritage site. The gravitational centre is Jemaa el-Fna, the square that fills every evening with food stalls, musicians and crowds, and which UNESCO separately recognises for its oral storytelling tradition. Around it run the souks of the Mouassine quarter, the Kasbah district to the south, and the Mellah, the old Jewish quarter, to the southeast. Outside the walls to the northwest lies Gueliz, the French-built ville nouvelle, which is flatter, greener, easier to walk and where most modern restaurants, galleries and shops sit.

Entry fees are standardised and modest. The Ministry of Culture charges foreign adults 100 dirhams each at Bahia Palace, El Badi Palace and the Saadian Tombs, with foreign children aged 7 to 13 paying 50 dirhams. Moroccan nationals and residents pay 30 dirhams and enter free every Friday and on the first day of national and religious holidays, so foreign visitors should not expect a free day. The Ben Youssef Madrasa, restored and reopened, charges foreign adults 50 dirhams, Moroccan adults 20 dirhams, children under 12 ten dirhams and groups of 21 or more 30 dirhams per head, opening 9am to 7pm daily and closing at 4.30pm during Ramadan. Le Jardin Secret in the Mouassine charges 100 dirhams to enter plus 40 dirhams for the tower, with tickets sold on site in dirhams or euros. Jardin Majorelle and the Musée Yves Saint Laurent Marrakech sell tickets online only through tickets.jardinmajorelle.com; the garden opens daily 8am to 6.30pm with last entry at 6pm, the Pierre Bergé Museum of Berber Arts 8.30am to 6pm, and the YSL museum 10am to 6pm with last entry at 5.30pm, every day except Wednesday. Koutoubia Mosque, the twelfth-century landmark beside the square, is closed to non-Muslims, so the visit is the exterior and gardens only.

Season matters more here than in most cities. Average highs reach 37.7C in July and 37.4C in August against 19.1C in January, and annual rainfall is only around 280mm, concentrated from February to April and again in November. March and April, and late September to mid-November, are the sensible windows. Anyone arriving in July or August should plan around the heat, front-loading sightseeing before 11am and treating mid-afternoon as indoor time.

The magnitude 6.8 Al Haouz earthquake of 8 September 2023 killed at least 2,960 people and damaged heritage in the medina, most visibly cutting the minaret of the Kharbouch mosque on Jemaa el-Fna roughly in half. The Mellah, with its older houses and narrow lanes, was the worst affected quarter inside the walls. Emergency consolidation and restoration works at sites including Koutoubia and Bahia Palace have been funded and were reviewed by UNESCO in 2024, and the main monuments are operating normally, but scaffolding and closed side streets remain part of the picture.

Getting in and around is straightforward. Menara Airport sits roughly six kilometres from the medina, the L19 shuttle bus runs into the centre for a low flat fare paid on board, and petit taxis are legally required to run meters even though many drivers will not. Most nationalities including US, UK, EU, Canadian and Australian passport holders enter visa free for up to 90 days. Bring cash, expect to be approached constantly, and treat every unsolicited offer of directions as a paid service.
destinations.what_great: The monument density is remarkable: Bahia Palace, El Badi, the Saadian Tombs and Ben Youssef Madrasa are all walkable from Jemaa el-Fna and cost 50 to 100 dirhams each for foreigners. Jemaa el-Fna at dusk is a genuine living tradition, not a staged show. Gueliz offers a calm, tree-lined counterweight to the souks. Food is cheap and excellent, the light is superb for photography from October to April, and the High Atlas begins less than an hour away.
destinations.what_ruined: The hassle is relentless and wears people down. Faux guides attach themselves near medina gates, walk you somewhere you did not ask to go, then demand payment. Henna women in and around Jemaa el-Fna start an unrequested design on your hand and then insist on a large fee. Photo handlers with monkeys and snakes charge aggressively after the shot. Petit taxi drivers routinely refuse the legally required meter and quote inflated flat rates, worse after dark. Souk haggling turns exhausting by day three, and July and August highs near 38C flatten any itinerary.
tips: Buy Jardin Majorelle and Musée Yves Saint Laurent tickets in advance at tickets.jardinmajorelle.com, because they are sold online only and the garden's last entry is 6pm.
Budget 100 dirhams per foreign adult for each of Bahia Palace, El Badi Palace and the Saadian Tombs, and carry small notes since ticket desks handle cash poorly.
Ben Youssef Madrasa costs foreign adults 50 dirhams and opens 9am to 7pm, but closes at 4.30pm during Ramadan, so check the dates before planning a late visit.
Insist on the meter in a petit taxi, and if the driver claims it is broken, get out and take the next one, as meters are legally required.
Visit between March and April or late September and mid-November, because July and August average highs of 37.7C make midday sightseeing genuinely unsafe for many people.
Never accept an unsolicited offer of directions inside the medina, and if hassle turns aggressive, ask for the Brigade Touristique, who patrol Jemaa el-Fna.

guide.title: Marrakech Practical Guide: Real Entry Fees, Airport Transfers, Seasons And Scam Defence
guide.summary: Month-by-month timing, Menara Airport transfers, medina navigation, verified monument fees, a realistic daily budget in US dollars, and a blunt section on the city's documented scams.
guide.body:
Timing is the single biggest decision. Marrakech averages highs of 37.7C in July and 37.4C in August, with lows still above 20C, and summers regularly push past 45C during heat events. January is the coolest month, averaging a high of 19.1C and a low of 5.9C, and riads without proper heating get genuinely cold at night. Rain is scarce, around 280mm a year, falling mostly February to April and again in November. The best windows are March and April, and late September to mid-November, when daytime highs sit in the mid twenties to low thirties. December to February works well for anyone who prefers cool weather and lower crowds, provided you pack layers for evenings. Ramadan shifts opening hours across the city, with Ben Youssef Madrasa closing at 4.30pm instead of 7pm, and many restaurants adjusting service.

Menara Airport is about six kilometres from the medina, which is a fifteen to twenty minute drive in normal traffic. The ALSA L19 shuttle bus runs from outside the terminal into the centre, stopping near Koutoubia for the walk to Jemaa el-Fna and continuing through Gueliz, with tickets bought from the driver in cash for a low flat fare. Petit taxis are the alternative and are the usual friction point: drivers at the airport habitually quote a flat rate rather than run the meter, and night rates are legitimately higher than day rates under the regional tariff system. Agree the number before the doors close, or walk to the road outside the terminal perimeter and flag a taxi that is already running its meter. Pre-booked riad transfers cost more than a taxi but remove the argument entirely, which is worth it on a late arrival with luggage.

Inside the walls, walking is the only real option, because the medina lanes are too narrow and too crowded for anything else. Distances are short, but navigation is the hard part, so download offline maps before arriving and accept that you will still get lost. Petit taxis connect the medina to Gueliz, the Menara Gardens and the Palmeraie quickly and cheaply when metered. Horse-drawn caleches operate from the square on fixed municipal routes and are a tourist ride rather than transport. The ONCF rail station in Gueliz links Marrakech to Casablanca and Rabat on the standard network, which is the practical way to add a second city.

On what to see, the Ministry of Culture sites are the backbone. Bahia Palace, an 8-hectare nineteenth-century complex of courtyards and painted ceilings, charges foreign adults 100 dirhams. El Badi Palace, the ruined Saadian showpiece, is the same 100 dirhams and rewards a slower visit for its scale and the storks nesting on the walls. The Saadian Tombs, the sixteenth-century necropolis rediscovered in 1917, also cost 100 dirhams and get very congested, so arrive at opening. Ben Youssef Madrasa charges foreign adults 50 dirhams and is arguably the best value single monument in the city. Le Jardin Secret costs 100 dirhams plus 40 dirhams for the tower and is a genuinely calm break in the middle of the souks. Jardin Majorelle is the city's most heavily booked attraction and sells tickets online only, so treat it as a fixed-time appointment rather than a walk-up. Koutoubia Mosque is closed to non-Muslims and should be treated as an exterior landmark, not a visit.

On budget, expect a lean independent trip to run roughly 55 to 85 US dollars per person per day, covering a simple riad room, street and cafe eating, local transport and one paid monument. A comfortable mid-range trip runs roughly 130 to 220 dollars per day, with a good riad, sit-down restaurant meals, two or three monuments and a taxi habit. Upper-end riads, private guides and day trips into the Atlas or the Agafay desert push past 350 dollars per day easily. Monuments themselves are a minor line item at 50 to 100 dirhams each. Accommodation and guided excursions are what move the total. Note that a per-person, per-night accommodation tax is added at checkout by most riads and hotels and is usually collected in cash, so keep dirhams aside for it.

On safety, Marrakech is not a violent-crime problem for visitors, it is a persistence problem. The faux guide pattern is the defining one: someone approaches near a medina gate, says the way ahead is closed or that they are heading the same direction, leads you somewhere, then demands payment. Decline firmly and keep walking. Henna applicators in and around Jemaa el-Fna will begin a design on an unsuspecting hand and then demand a large fee, and photo handlers with monkeys and snakes work the same way. Anything placed on you or started for you is a bill. Petit taxi meter refusal is the most common daily annoyance and the fix is simply to take a different taxi. The Brigade Touristique patrols the main square and tourist areas and takes harassment complaints seriously, so naming them usually ends a confrontation. Carry cash in small denominations, keep valuables out of open bags in crowded souk lanes, and be aware that some medina streets damaged in the 2023 earthquake remain closed or under scaffolding.

rating_rationale.overall: The concentration of genuinely first-rank monuments inside a compact walled medina, most charging only 50 to 100 dirhams for foreign adults, is exceptional value for a city of this scale.
rating_rationale.safety: Violent crime against visitors is rare and the Brigade Touristique is active around Jemaa el-Fna, but persistent commission-driven hassle, faux guides and taxi meter refusal are documented and constant.
rating_rationale.value: Ministry of Culture monuments cost 100 dirhams for foreign adults, the airport bus runs about 30 dirhams and food is cheap, so daily costs stay low even when accommodation is not.
