destinations.name: Medellín
destinations.summary: Medellin sells itself as the City of Eternal Spring, and the climate, Metro system, and Comuna 13 transformation really do deliver, but the same qualities that drew a wave of digital nomads have pushed rents past Bogota's and turned parts of El Poblado into a bubble disconnected from the rest of the city, while dating-app druggings and targeted crime against tourists remain a real, documented risk.
destinations.headline: Medellin in 2026: eternal spring, a genuinely good Metro, and a dating-app drugging problem that is not hype
destinations.body:
Medellin's nickname, the City of Eternal Spring, is earned. The city sits at roughly 4,900 feet and holds a year-round average near 22.5 degrees Celsius (72.5 F), with daytime highs typically between 26 and 28 C and lows around 16 to 18 C every month of the year. There is no real winter or summer, just a bimodal wet-dry pattern, with the rainiest stretches from April to May and September to November, and drier weather from December to March and July to August. That consistency is the single biggest reason the city has become what it has become.

What it has become is the unofficial Latin American capital of digital nomadism, and the numbers show it. Colombia's digital nomad visa, introduced in late 2022, allows stays of up to two years for remote workers who can show income of roughly three times the Colombian minimum wage, about COP 5.25 million per month in 2026, plus health insurance and six months of remote work history. An estimated 8,300 digital nomads a month have been arriving in the city, and Airbnb and Vrbo listings jumped 45 percent in a single year to over 12,000. The predictable result: Medellin overtook Bogota in 2025 as Colombia's most expensive rental market, with rents in El Poblado, Laureles, and parts of Envigado up more than 25 percent since 2020. Locals in those neighborhoods are increasingly priced out, and there is organized pushback against gentrification and the sexual tourism that has grown alongside it.

The transit system is one of the city's genuine, uncomplicated wins. The Metro, Colombia's only metro system, connects with the Metrocable gondola lines that climb into the hillside comunas, giving residents of formerly cut-off, violent neighborhoods a fast, affordable commute into downtown. As of January 2026 the standard Metro fare is COP 3,820 with a Civica smart card (COP 4,400 for a single occasional-use ticket), and most Metrocable lines are included in that fare if used within a 90-minute transfer window, the exception being Line L to Parque Arvi, which costs an extra COP 13,700 as a standalone tourist attraction. Riding the cable car up to Santo Domingo or Villa Sierra remains one of the best, cheapest ways to actually see how the city works.

Comuna 13, once one of the most dangerous barrios in Medellin, is now the city's most visited tourist attraction, rebuilt around outdoor escalators, murals, and hip-hop culture. Guided graffiti tours run around 80,000 to 120,000 COP (roughly 20 to 30 USD) for three to four hours including metro transport and snacks, though budget options exist for as little as 10 to 18 USD. It is a real transformation story and a legitimately good afternoon, but it is also now thoroughly a tourist product, with vendors, paid photo ops, and crowds to match.

Now the part travel bloggers undersell: safety. The US State Department keeps Colombia at Level 3, Reconsider Travel, and while Medellin is not in a Do Not Travel zone, the US Embassy has repeatedly and specifically warned about dating-app-related drugging and robbery targeting foreigners in the city. In late 2023 eight US citizens died in Medellin in a two-month span under suspicious circumstances tied to scopolamine, known locally as devil's breath, a drug that can incapacitate victims and erase memory; the pattern typically starts with a match on Tinder, Bumble, or Grindr. In 2024, roughly 39 tourists died in Medellin, about half of them American, though that figure includes accidents, cosmetic-surgery complications, overdoses, and suicides alongside homicides, not all violent crime. The local mantra, no dar papaya, meaning don't give away a papaya, don't make yourself an easy target, sums up the practical reality: keep phones and jewelry out of sight, meet dating-app matches in busy public places only, and don't assume the eternal-spring weather means the eternal-spring city is uniformly safe.
destinations.what_great: The climate genuinely never gets old, the Metro and Metrocable are clean, cheap, and actually useful for tourists and locals alike, and Comuna 13's turnaround from combat zone to open-air street art gallery is one of the more remarkable urban transformation stories in the hemisphere. Add a Guatape day trip with the surreal Piedra del Penol rock and a lakeside colonial town, plus a genuinely low cost of living that still stretches further than most of Latin America, and it is easy to see why so many visitors extend a week into a month.
destinations.what_ruined: The nomad boom has hollowed out affordability in exactly the neighborhoods (El Poblado, increasingly Laureles) most tourists stay in, so you are often paying gentrified prices for a diluted, expat-bubble version of the city. Layer on a documented, specific, ongoing risk of dating-app drugging and robbery targeting foreigners, plus a broader Level 3 State Department advisory, and Medellin demands a level of street-smarts and caution that the eternal-spring marketing conveniently leaves out.
tips: Metro fare with a Civica card is COP 3,820 (about $0.95) as of January 2026; a single occasional-use ticket is COP 4,400. Most Metrocable lines are covered within a 90-minute transfer, except Line L to Parque Arvi which costs an extra COP 13,700.

The regulated flat taxi fare from Jose Maria Cordova Airport (MDE) to El Poblado is around COP 118,000 to 128,000 (roughly $30 to $32); a shared colectivo van runs about COP 17,000 to 27,000 and takes roughly 25 to 40 minutes.

On dating apps, meet matches only in busy public places for the first time, never at your hotel or their home, and trust your gut if something feels off; scopolamine-related druggings tied to Tinder, Bumble, and Grindr matches have been directly linked to multiple US citizen deaths since 2023.

Follow 'no dar papaya': keep your phone off the street curb, skip visible jewelry and watches, and don't flash cash. Phone theft at gunpoint by motorcycle-riding thieves is the most common tourist crime in the city.

El Poblado is the polished, nomad-heavy, most expensive base; Laureles is quieter, more residential, and increasingly gentrifying too; Envigado sits further out but is calmer and cheaper. Pick based on how much expat-bubble you want.
Rainiest months are April to May and September to November; driest are December to March and July to August, though showers are usually brief rather than all-day.
A Comuna 13 graffiti tour runs roughly COP 80,000 to 120,000 ($20 to $30) for 3 to 4 hours including metro transport and snacks; budget self-guided or smaller tours can run as low as $10 to $18.

Restaurants add a 10 percent propina voluntaria (voluntary tip) to the bill and will ask if you want it included; it's optional and there's no social penalty for declining, though most people accept it.

Guatape is reached by bus from Terminal del Norte (Metro Line A, Caribe station); tickets run about COP 21,000 to 24,000 one-way ($5 to $6), with the ride taking just under two hours; get off early for Piedra del Penol before continuing into town.

guide.title: Medellin travel guide 2026: getting around, where to stay, and staying safe
guide.summary: A practical guide to landing at MDE, using the Metro and Metrocable, choosing between El Poblado, Laureles, and Envigado, and the safety habits that actually matter in a city with a real dating-app drugging problem.
guide.body:
Jose Maria Cordova International Airport (MDE) sits up in the hills about 35 to 45 minutes outside the city center, not in it, so budget transfer time and cost into your first and last day. The city-regulated taxi fare into El Poblado is a flat COP 118,000 to 128,000 (about $30 to $32, tolls included), booked at the official taxi counter inside the terminal. Cheaper options exist: a shared colectivo van runs roughly COP 17,000 to 27,000, and a public bus is around COP 17,000 to 20,000, both taking 40 minutes to an hour depending on traffic. Private app-based transfers and Uber also operate, though Uber's legal status in Colombia has fluctuated, so have a backup plan.

Once you're in the city, use the Metro. It is Colombia's only metro system and one of the best-run pieces of public infrastructure in Latin America, connecting downtown with the Metrocable gondola lines that climb into the hillside comunas. As of January 2026, a ride costs COP 3,820 with a rechargeable Civica card (get one at any station) or COP 4,400 for a single-use ticket. Most Metrocable transfers are included in that fare within a 90-minute window; the exception is Line L out to Parque Arvi, a separate tourist line costing an extra COP 13,700 round trip. Riding a cable car up to Santo Domingo gives you a view over the whole Aburra Valley and a look at neighborhoods that were, within living memory, no-go zones.

Where to stay comes down to how much of the international-bubble version of Medellin you want. El Poblado is the default tourist and nomad base: walkable, full of coworking spaces, good restaurants, and nightlife, but also the epicenter of the rent spike that made Medellin Colombia's most expensive rental market in 2025, and the neighborhood most associated with sexual tourism and scam targeting. Laureles is a calmer, more residential alternative with a strong local food and cafe scene, increasingly popular with longer-term nomads who want less of an expat echo chamber, though prices there are climbing too. Envigado, technically a separate municipality just south, is quieter and cheaper still, with easy Metro access into the center.

Safety in Medellin is not about avoiding the city, it's about specific habits. The single most important one: if you use dating apps, meet any match for the first time in a busy public place only, never at a private residence or hotel room, and leave immediately if anything feels off. This is not generic caution, it follows a documented pattern behind multiple tourist deaths from scopolamine drugging since 2023, serious enough that the US Embassy issued direct, repeated warnings about it. Beyond that, follow the local rule of no dar papaya: keep your phone off the street, don't wear visible jewelry or flash cash, and don't walk distracted near the curb, since phone snatching by motorcycle-riding thieves is the most common tourist crime. The country overall sits at US State Department Level 3, Reconsider Travel, though Medellin itself is not in a Do Not Travel zone.

For day trips, Guatape is the standard: catch a bus from Terminal del Norte (reachable via Metro Line A to Caribe station) for about COP 21,000 to 24,000 one-way, roughly a 90-minute to two-hour ride, and get off early to climb Piedra del Penol, a granite monolith with a 649-step staircase and a panoramic view of the reservoir, before continuing into the colorful lakeside town itself. Comuna 13 is the closer-in option, reachable directly by Metro to San Javier station, with guided graffiti tours running COP 80,000 to 120,000 for three to four hours. For money, Colombian pesos are the only realistic way to pay outside upscale El Poblado spots; ATMs are widely available but often charge steep withdrawal fees, so consolidate withdrawals rather than making frequent small ones, and carry small bills since street vendors and older shops rarely break large notes.

rating_rationale.overall: The core attractions (climate, Metro/Metrocable, Comuna 13, Guatape) are genuinely excellent and well worth the trip, which keeps this high, but the gentrified expat-bubble feel in El Poblado and the real safety overhead needed to enjoy the city responsibly keep it from a 5.
rating_rationale.safety: This is not generic big-city caution: the US Embassy has issued specific, repeated warnings about scopolamine drugging via dating apps tied to multiple tourist deaths, the country sits at State Department Level 3, and cell-phone robbery at gunpoint is common enough that locals coined a phrase for avoiding it. Most visits are fine, but the risk profile is real and specific, not theoretical.
rating_rationale.value: Medellin overtook Bogota as Colombia's most expensive rental market in 2025 and El Poblado prices now resemble a mid-tier US or European city for lodging and nomad-oriented services, but public transit, Comuna 13 tours, and the Guatape day trip remain genuinely cheap, so value swings hard depending on which neighborhood and lifestyle you choose.

destinations.name: Mexico City
destinations.summary: One of the best food and museum cities on earth, sitting at 2,240 meters where the air is thin and often dirty, in the middle of a housing crunch that has locals furious at the foreigners flooding Roma and Condesa.
destinations.headline: Mexico City in 2026: incredible food and culture, thin air, and a gentrification backlash you'll feel
destinations.body:
Mexico City earns its reputation. The food scene runs from five-peso street tacos to multiple World's 50 Best restaurants, the museum density rivals Paris, and neighborhoods like Roma Norte and Condesa are genuinely beautiful, tree-lined and walkable in a way few Latin American capitals manage. It is also enormous, chaotic, and sitting at 2,240 meters above sea level, which means roughly 25 percent less oxygen than at sea level. Most visitors need 24 to 72 hours to adjust, and mild headaches, breathlessness on stairs, or fatigue on day one are normal, not a medical emergency.

Most travelers land at AICM (Mexico City International Airport), a short metro or taxi ride from the center. Some budget carriers now fly into AIFA (Felipe Ángeles), a newer airport about 45 kilometers and roughly 45 minutes north of downtown on a former air force base, which is cheaper to fly into but adds real transit time and cost. For entry, the FMM tourist permit is free if you're arriving by air on a trip under seven days, or free by land for stays of a week or less; immigration officers can grant up to 180 days at their discretion, and a paper FMM for longer or replacement purposes runs about 983 pesos, roughly 54 dollars.

Getting around the city is one of the genuine wins. The Metro is a flat 5 pesos per ride, a price that has not moved since 2013 and is heavily subsidized (the real cost per ride is closer to 13 pesos). A rechargeable Metro card costs 15 pesos, or 20 pesos total if you buy it with your first ride included. It is fast and cheap but also crowded and not a place for visible valuables. For the airport and late nights, Uber is the better call: it typically runs 50 to 70 percent cheaper than the official taxi kiosks inside the terminal, and it sidesteps the touts who approach arriving passengers offering unofficial rides, a well-documented scam vector at AICM. If you do take a taxi, use the staffed kiosk inside the terminal, not someone who walks up to you.

The real friction points go beyond altitude. Air quality is a genuine issue, particularly in the dry season from November through May, when thermal inversions trap pollution in the valley the city sits in. Tap water is not safe to drink, full stop, about 70 percent of Mexico City residents avoid it too, and that includes ice made from tap water at less careful establishments, so stick to bottled or purified water even for brushing teeth if you're being cautious. The city also sits on an old lakebed that amplifies earthquake shaking by a factor of 5 to 50 compared to solid ground; the September 19, 2017 magnitude 7.1 quake killed 326 people, 187 of them in the city, and a magnitude 7.7 quake in September 2022 also caused damage and deaths. Building codes have been tightened repeatedly since 1985, but this is a seismically live city, not a hypothetical risk.

The newest friction is social, not physical. The remote-work influx since the pandemic has driven serious displacement: rents in Condesa rose about 17 percent between April 2023 and April 2025, one-bedroom rents in the same window rose around 30 percent, and the surrounding Miguel Hidalgo borough saw rents jump nearly 98 percent. Airbnb listings in the Roma-Condesa-Hipódromo core rose from about 2,900 in 2019 to over 5,000 by 2023. That tension boiled into visible anti-gentrification protests in July 2025, and the mayor announced a 14-point plan in response, including capping rent increases at inflation. None of this makes the city unsafe for visitors, the US State Department keeps Mexico City at a Level 2, exercise-increased-caution rating, similar to much of Western Europe, but tourists staying in Roma or Condesa are, whether they like it or not, part of the story locals are angry about.
destinations.what_great: The food is worth the trip on its own, from taco stands to internationally ranked tasting menus, and museum-going here is a full-day-after-full-day activity with the anthropology museum, Bellas Artes, Frida Kahlo's Casa Azul and dozens more all genuinely world-class. Roma Norte and Condesa are as walkable and photogenic as any neighborhood in the Americas, the Metro is absurdly cheap at 5 pesos a ride, and a day trip to the Teotihuacán pyramids is both easy (a public bus from the Autobuses del Norte terminal) and genuinely awe-inspiring.
destinations.what_ruined: The altitude and pollution combo means your first day or two may involve headaches and shortness of breath just from carrying luggage up stairs, tap water is off-limits so you're buying bottled water constantly, and the city sits on ground that amplifies earthquakes, a real risk given the 2017 and 2022 quakes killed people here within the last decade. On top of that, the digital-nomad boom has pushed rents up double digits in the neighborhoods tourists most want to stay in, sparked actual street protests against foreigners in mid-2025, and left a lingering awkwardness that visitors staying in an Airbnb in Condesa are, statistically, part of the problem residents are protesting.
tips: The Metro is a flat 5 pesos per ride regardless of distance, unchanged since 2013; buy a rechargeable card for 15 pesos (20 pesos total with your first ride included).
Give yourself 24 to 72 hours to adjust to the 2,240-meter altitude before pushing hard on hiking or heavy exercise; about 25 percent less oxygen than sea level is normal to feel.

Do not drink the tap water, and be wary of ice at less careful spots; about 70 percent of Mexico City residents also avoid tap water, so bottled or purified is the norm citywide, not a tourist-only precaution.
Skip the taxi touts inside AICM arrivals; use the staffed official taxi kiosk or, cheaper, order an Uber, which typically runs 50 to 70 percent less than the official airport taxi rate.
The FMM tourist permit is free for stays of 7 days or less; for longer stays officers can grant up to 180 days, and a paper FMM replacement or extension costs about 983 pesos (roughly $54 USD).
Visit in the dry season, November through April, for the best weather and air quality; the wet season runs June through October with heavy afternoon downpours, and September is the wettest month.

Tip 10 to 15 percent at casual spots and taquerías (rounding up is fine), 15 percent or more at upscale restaurants; check your bill for 'propina incluida' or 'servicio incluido' since a tip is not automatically added otherwise.

Teotihuacán is an easy, cheap day trip: take Metro Line 5 to Autobuses del Norte, then a bus for about 75 pesos one-way (roughly every 15 to 20 minutes, 6am to 9pm); site admission for foreign visitors is 210 pesos under 2026 rates.

guide.title: Mexico City travel guide 2026: airports, neighborhoods, and how not to get sick or scammed
guide.summary: The practical version: how to get in from MEX or AIFA, which neighborhood to actually book, what to eat off the street versus not, and how to do Teotihuacán without an overpriced tour.
guide.body:
Most flights land at AICM, Mexico City's main airport, split into Terminal 1 and the newer Terminal 2 connected by a free shuttle and the Metrobús. A growing number of budget routes instead use AIFA (Felipe Ángeles International), a newer airport built on a former air force base about 45 kilometers and roughly 45 minutes north of downtown in Zumpango, State of Mexico; fares can be cheaper but factor in the extra time and a bus or car for the transfer. On entry, most tourists get the FMM permit free if flying in for a stay under seven days (it's baked into your airfare) or free crossing by land under a week; immigration can authorize up to 180 days at their discretion, and a paper FMM extension or replacement runs about 983 pesos, close to 54 US dollars.

Once you're in the city, the Metro is the backbone of getting around: 5 pesos flat per ride, a price frozen since 2013 thanks to a government subsidy (the real cost is nearer 13 pesos). Buy a rechargeable card for 15 pesos, or 20 pesos with your first ride bundled in. It's efficient but can be genuinely packed at rush hour, so watch your bag. For the airport run, late nights, or anywhere you're carrying luggage, Uber is both safer and cheaper, running 50 to 70 percent below the official taxi kiosk rate; if you do want a taxi, use the staffed kiosk inside the terminal rather than anyone who approaches you in arrivals, which is a known scam setup.

Where to stay comes down to Roma Norte and Condesa for walkability, cafes, and nightlife (also the epicenter of the digital-nomad rent spikes locals are protesting, so expect higher prices and some social friction), Polanco for upscale and corporate travel, and the Centro Histórico for proximity to the Zócalo and colonial-era sights at the cost of more noise and tourist density. All three are well connected to the Metro and Metrobús network.

On food safety, street food is a legitimate part of the experience, not something to avoid wholesale, but go where there's a line of locals and high turnover, and skip anything sitting out at room temperature. The bigger universal rule is water: don't drink tap water anywhere in the city, avoid ice at places that look like they're not filtering it, and stick to bottled or purified water including for brushing your teeth if you want to be careful. Roughly 70 percent of Mexico City residents avoid their own tap water too, so this isn't tourist paranoia, it's local practice.

The single best day trip is Teotihuacán. Skip the marked-up organized tours and take Metro Line 5 to Autobuses del Norte station, then catch a bus from Module 8 (Autobuses Teotihuacanos) for about 75 pesos one-way; buses run every 15 to 20 minutes from 6am to 9pm and take roughly 60 to 90 minutes. Site admission for foreign visitors is 210 pesos under the 2026 fee schedule. On money and tipping, 10 to 15 percent is standard at casual restaurants and taquerías, 15 percent or more at nicer places, and you should always check the bottom of your bill for 'propina incluida' since tips are not automatically added by default. Cash tips are generally preferred over adding the tip on a card, even where card payment is common.

rating_rationale.overall: World-class food, museums and neighborhood walkability pull this toward the top of the scale, but altitude adjustment, real air quality problems in dry season, and genuine seismic risk keep it from a perfect score.
rating_rationale.safety: The US State Department rates Mexico City Level 2, exercise increased caution, on par with much of Western Europe for the tourist core, but airport taxi scams, petty theft on the crowded Metro, and a documented earthquake history (326 dead in 2017, deaths again in 2022) are real, not theoretical, considerations.
rating_rationale.value: A 5-peso metro ride, cheap street food, and a sub-$15 round trip to Teotihuacán by public bus make this an exceptional-value city for the quality on offer, though the same gentrification driving up Roma and Condesa rents is starting to push mid-range accommodation prices toward what you'd pay in a US city.

destinations.name: Nairobi
destinations.summary: Nairobi puts a real national park inside the capital and a real eTA hurdle before you land, honest costs and honest crime risk included.
destinations.headline: Nairobi: The Only Capital With Rhinos at the City Limits, and a Visa Hurdle to Match
destinations.body:
Nairobi is the only capital city in the world with a full national park inside its boundaries, and that single fact does more to explain the place than any tourism slogan. Nairobi National Park sits just a few kilometers from skyscrapers in Upper Hill and the Central Business District, and it is genuinely possible to photograph a giraffe or a black rhino with the city's glass towers in the background. Non-resident adults pay $80 to enter, non-resident children and students pay $40, and Kenya Wildlife Service now applies that rate year-round instead of the old seasonal pricing, with tickets purchased online through the eCitizen platform rather than cash at the gate.

Getting into the country changed meaningfully in 2024 and the shift still trips up travelers in 2026. Kenya scrapped visa-on-arrival and now requires an Electronic Travel Authorization, applied for in advance at etakenya.go.ke. The fee runs about $30, approval typically comes back within roughly 72 hours, and immigration officials expect it done before you board, not at the JKIA counter. You'll need six months of passport validity, a digital photo, and proof of accommodation and onward travel.

Jomo Kenyatta International Airport sits about 15 kilometers southeast of downtown, and the drive in can take anywhere from 17 minutes with clear roads to 45 minutes or more once Nairobi's notorious traffic kicks in. Uber and Bolt both operate at the airport and are the least stressful option, a private car into town runs roughly KSH 2,500 to 3,000, call it $19 to $23 at 2026 exchange rates, with minivans closer to KSH 4,500 to 5,000 for larger groups. Budget travelers can take the KBS Route 34 airport bus for KES 50 to 100, though it's slower and less predictable.

Safety in Nairobi is genuinely a mixed picture and worth being honest about. The Central Business District sees the highest concentration of reported incidents, including armed robbery targeting vehicles stopped in traffic, and walking there alone after dark is a bad idea. Pickpocketing and bag snatching are common in crowded markets and on public transport. Informal settlements like Kibera and Mathare carry both higher crime risk and flood exposure during heavy rains. None of that describes Karen, Langata, or Westlands, the neighborhoods where most visitors actually stay: Karen and Langata are upscale, close to the national park and the Giraffe Centre, and Westlands has become the expat and business hub with hotels, restaurants, and malls that feel like an entirely different city than the CBD after sunset.

Most people pass through Nairobi on their way to the Maasai Mara, and that leg is where the real money goes. The Mara sits about 224 kilometers southwest of the city by road, or a roughly 45-minute hop from Wilson Airport costing $130 to $200 one way. Mara park fees for non-residents run $100 per person per day in the January to June low season and jump to $200 per day from July through December, stacked on top of whatever you already paid to see Nairobi National Park. Full safari packages, lodging included, range from roughly $380 to over $1,100 per person per day depending on tier, and a 3-day fly-in trip can start around $1,850 per person. The Kenyan shilling has held fairly steady near KES 129 to the US dollar through 2026, with inflation drifting between about 4.4 percent in March and 6.7 percent in May before easing to 6.4 percent in June, so your dollar goes further in the city itself than the safari math suggests.
destinations.what_great:
Nairobi's single best trick is proximity: you can eat breakfast downtown and be photographing rhinos and giraffes inside Nairobi National Park within twenty minutes, something no other capital on earth offers. The skyline-behind-wildlife shot at the park is not a gimmick, it's a real, repeatable thing you can go see. Westlands has genuinely good restaurants and a real expat and business energy, and Karen and Langata feel worlds away from downtown traffic while staying close to the park and the Giraffe Centre. As a base for onward safari travel, Nairobi is unmatched, Wilson Airport puts you in the Maasai Mara in about 45 minutes, and JKIA connects to most of the continent.

The eTA system, annoying as it is, is at least fast and predictable once you understand it: apply a week out, pay the roughly $30 fee, and you typically have an answer in about three days rather than gambling on an arrival queue.
destinations.what_ruined:
The CBD after dark is the honest downside here. Reported incidents cluster there, including armed robbery targeting cars stuck in traffic, and it's not a place to wander on foot once the sun goes down. Petty theft, pickpocketing, and bag snatching are routine in crowded markets and on matatus and buses, so situational awareness isn't optional. Kibera and Mathare carry real flood risk in heavy rains on top of higher crime exposure, and they are not tourist stops.

Costs stack up fast once you leave the city. Nairobi National Park's own $80 non-resident adult fee is reasonable, but the moment you add a Maasai Mara leg you're looking at $100 to $200 per person per day in park fees alone, on top of $130 to $200 one-way flights and safari packages that commonly run $380 to $1,100 per person per day. None of that is a scam, it's just the real price of the classic Kenya trip, and budget travelers researching a cheap Nairobi-plus-safari combo will be disappointed by the math.
tips: Apply for Kenya's eTA at least 7 days before travel at etakenya.go.ke, it costs around $30 and typically clears in about 72 hours, don't wait until the airport.
Book and pay your Nairobi National Park ticket in advance through the KWS eCitizen system, non-resident adults pay $80 and children/students pay $40, a flat rate year-round.
Skip walking around the CBD after dark, armed robbery targeting cars stuck in traffic is a real, reported risk there, base yourself in Karen, Langata, or Westlands instead.
Use Uber or Bolt from JKIA rather than a random taxi tout, expect roughly KSH 2,500-3,000 (about $19-23) for a car into town, more once you hit traffic.

If Nairobi is your springboard to the Maasai Mara, budget for the 224km road trip or a roughly 45-minute Wilson Airport flight ($130-200 one way), plus separate Mara park fees ($100/day low season, $200/day high season for non-residents) on top of what you already paid at Nairobi National Park.
Keep an eye on the shilling, it has been holding near KES 129 to the dollar through 2026 with inflation bouncing between about 4.4% and 6.7%, so build in a small budget cushion.

guide.title: Nairobi Travel Guide: Getting Around, When to Go, and Where to Stay
guide.summary: A practical rundown of Nairobi's neighborhoods, transport options, seasonal timing, and where the real costs hide.
guide.body:
Base yourself in Westlands if you want restaurants, nightlife, and easy access to malls and coworking-style cafes, or in Karen or Langata if you'd rather wake up closer to Nairobi National Park and the Giraffe Centre with a quieter, more residential feel. Both areas sit well clear of the Central Business District's after-dark risk profile, and most hotels and Airbnbs aimed at foreign visitors cluster in one of the three.

Getting around the city itself means picking between Uber or Bolt, which are widely available and the easiest way to avoid taxi-tout hassles, and matatus, the privately run minibuses that are cheap but chaotic and best attempted once you already have your bearings. Traffic is the real variable in any Nairobi plan: a trip that takes 17 minutes at 6am can take 45 minutes or more during rush hour, so build slack into any airport run or same-day itinerary.

Timing your visit matters more for the safari leg than for the city. Maasai Mara park fees for non-residents double in the July to December high season compared to the January to June low season, so travelers chasing value should lean toward the first half of the year if the calendar allows it, weighing that against wildlife migration timing. In the city, pack for cool mornings and evenings, Nairobi sits at high altitude and temperatures swing more than travelers expect from an equatorial country.

Money-wise, the eTA fee and the Nairobi National Park ticket are both worth paying online in advance rather than trying to sort out at the border or the gate. Carry small shilling notes for markets and tips and lean on cards for hotels and bigger purchases, and keep in mind the shilling has been trading close to KES 129 to the dollar through 2026, so quick mental math at that rate is usually close enough for day-to-day spending decisions.

rating_rationale.overall: Unmatched wildlife-in-a-capital novelty and safari-gateway convenience, offset by real safety friction and stacking costs once you leave the park gate.
rating_rationale.safety: Safe in Karen, Langata and Westlands with normal awareness, but the CBD after dark and informal settlements carry real, documented risk.
rating_rationale.value: City costs and entry fees are transparent and reasonable, but Maasai Mara add-ons ($100-200/day park fees plus $380-1,100/day safaris) make the full trip pricier than it first looks.

destinations.name: New Orleans
destinations.summary: New Orleans pairs French and Spanish colonial architecture, live jazz on nearly every block, and some of the country's best Creole and Cajun food with real, current safety and weather planning issues that visitors should not ignore.
destinations.headline: New Orleans 2026 Travel Guide: French Quarter Culture, Jazz and Food, Plus Bourbon Street Security and Hurricane Season Facts
destinations.body:
New Orleans remains one of the most architecturally distinct cities in the United States, with the French Quarter's wrought iron balconies, courtyards, and Creole townhouses dating largely to Spanish colonial rebuilding after the 1788 and 1794 fires. Live music is not a tourist add on but a daily civic fact, with brass bands, second lines, and clubs on Frenchmen Street running most nights of the week, and the city's jazz history is documented at the New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park and the Presbytere and Cabildo museums on Jackson Square. Food culture spans Creole fine dining, po boys, beignets at Cafe du Monde, and a dense concentration of James Beard recognized kitchens.

Safety planning has changed since the January 1, 2025 truck attack on Bourbon Street, which killed 15 people plus the attacker and injured dozens more. Investigations found that permanent bollards meant to block vehicle access had been removed for repairs ahead of the Super Bowl and were not back in place at the time of the attack. Since then the city has installed a mix of fixed and movable steel bollards, heavy planters, and reinforced gates at entry points to the pedestrian zone, spending roughly 167,000 dollars on a mobile bollard fleet, though as of the one year anniversary in January 2026 city officials and French Quarter business owners were still pushing for a permanent, funded security plan rather than the current stopgap barriers.

Other friction points are more mundane but just as worth planning around. Atlantic hurricane season runs June 1 through November 30, with the highest activity typically mid August through October, and forecasters for 2026 called for a near normal to slightly below normal season, which is still enough to disrupt flights and hotel stays with little notice. Summer visitors face serious heat and humidity, with July heat index values commonly reaching the mid 100s Fahrenheit and average relative humidity around 73 to 79 percent. In February 2026, New Orleans police publicly warned Carnival season visitors after a French Quarter pickpocketing spree, arresting five suspects and recovering 71 stolen cellphones in a single weekend.

The city's post Katrina flood defense system, the 14.5 billion dollar Hurricane and Storm Damage Risk Reduction System completed after 2005, held through Hurricane Isaac in 2012 and Category 4 Hurricane Ida in 2021, but engineering reporting in 2025 and 2026 found the levees and floodwalls are sinking due to subsidence and sea level rise, with a 2023 Army Corps reevaluation estimating roughly 3.5 billion dollars in additional work needed over 50 years to sustain protection.
destinations.what_great: New Orleans delivers a genuinely rare combination of dense, walkable historic architecture, live jazz and brass band music as a daily street level experience rather than a staged show, and a food scene, from Creole fine dining to po boys and beignets, that regularly draws national recognition. The compact French Quarter and Garden District, the St. Charles Avenue streetcar line running since 1835, and year round festivals from Mardi Gras to Jazz Fest give visitors an unusually high density of things to do within a small, walkable footprint.
destinations.what_ruined: The honest friction points are real rather than exaggerated. Bourbon Street security is still a work in progress a year after the January 2025 truck attack, with temporary bollards and barriers standing in for the permanent plan officials have not yet funded, and French Quarter pickpocketing remains active enough that police issued a public warning during Carnival season 2026. Summer heat index values regularly hit the low 100s Fahrenheit, hurricane season stretches from June through November and can disrupt travel with little warning, and the post Katrina levee system, while it has held through major storms since 2012, is documented as sinking and underfunded for the maintenance it needs.
tips: A single RTA bus or streetcar ride costs 1.25 dollars, and a 1 day Jazzy Pass covering unlimited streetcar, bus, and ferry rides costs 3 dollars, per the New Orleans RTA fare page.

Open containers of alcohol in plastic to go cups, not glass or metal, are legal on French Quarter streets and sidewalks under city ordinance, but this exemption ends at the Quarter's boundaries of Rampart Street, Canal Street, Esplanade Avenue, and the Mississippi River.

Atlantic hurricane season runs June 1 through November 30, with peak risk mid August through October, so trip insurance with hurricane or cancellation coverage is worth checking for visits in that window.
The National WWII Museum is open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily except Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, and Mardi Gras Day, with general admission starting at 27 dollars.

In February 2026 New Orleans police reported arresting five suspected pickpockets and recovering 71 stolen cellphones from a single weekend French Quarter spree, so keeping phones and wallets in front pockets rather than back pockets or open bags is a practical precaution during Carnival season.

guide.title: New Orleans Practical Travel Guide 2026
guide.summary: How to get to New Orleans, when to go, where to stay, and what to budget, balanced against current Bourbon Street security status and hurricane season timing.
guide.body: Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport connects to most major U.S. hubs and sits about 15 miles from downtown, with rideshare or the airport shuttle the simplest way in. The most comfortable weather runs roughly late October through April, avoiding both peak hurricane season, June through November with the highest activity mid August through October, and the worst summer heat, when July heat index values commonly reach the mid 100s Fahrenheit with humidity averaging around 73 to 79 percent. Mardi Gras and the Jazz and Heritage Festival in spring draw the largest crowds and the highest hotel rates, so booking months ahead matters for those windows. For lodging, the French Quarter puts visitors closest to Bourbon Street, Jackson Square, and Frenchmen Street music clubs but is the loudest and priciest option, while the Garden District and areas along the St. Charles Avenue streetcar line offer a quieter, still walkable alternative with easy transit access. Budget travelers can rely on the RTA's 1.25 dollar single fares and 3 dollar day pass to cover streetcars, buses, and the ferry, and can eat well cheaply on po boys and neighborhood Creole spots rather than tourist strip restaurants. Must do activities include a St. Charles streetcar ride, a walk through the French Quarter's Spanish colonial architecture, live brass band or jazz sets on Frenchmen Street, and the National WWII Museum, open daily 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. with admission starting at 27 dollars. What to avoid: walking Bourbon Street late at night alone or with an unattended drink, given active pickpocketing warnings and the unfinished permanent security plan a year after the January 2025 truck attack, and booking a trip during peak hurricane season without checking cancellation or weather coverage on travel insurance.

rating_rationale.overall: The architecture, music, and food scene are genuinely exceptional and rarely matched elsewhere in the United States, which keeps the overall editorial score high despite real safety and weather caveats.
rating_rationale.safety: Ongoing pickpocketing warnings, an unfinished permanent security plan for Bourbon Street a year after the 2025 attack, and hurricane season exposure justify a middle rating rather than a top score.
rating_rationale.value: Transit is inexpensive, a 1.25 dollar single ride and 3 dollar day pass, and food ranges from cheap po boys to splurge dining, though hotel rates spike hard around Mardi Gras and Jazz Fest.

destinations.name: Oaxaca
destinations.summary: Colonial capital and Zapotec heartland in southern Mexico, known for mezcal, mole, Monte Alban, and two festival peaks that overwhelm the city's capacity.
destinations.headline: Oaxaca Review: World-Class Food and Ruins, Priced and Crowded to the Limit in Festival Season
destinations.body:
Oaxaca de Juarez is the capital of Oaxaca state in southern Mexico, and the city centre together with the archaeological site of Monte Alban was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987. The grid of the Centro Historico is Spanish colonial town planning built low and heavy for an earthquake zone, anchored by the Zocalo, the pedestrian Andador Macedonio Alcala, and the Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzman. The former convent beside the church holds the Museo de las Culturas de Oaxaca, which INAH lists at 210 pesos general admission and 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and residents, open Tuesday to Saturday 10:00 to 17:30 with last entry at 17:00 and Sunday 10:00 to 15:30, closed Mondays.

Monte Alban itself sits on a levelled ridge about 10 kilometres from the centre and is open daily 8:00 to 17:00 with last admission at 16:00. INAH's official rate is 210 pesos for general admission and 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and residents, under the national fee schedule effective January 1, 2026. Sundays are free for Mexicans and legal residents, which also makes Sunday the most crowded day. Mitla, about 45 kilometres southeast and famous for its geometric stone fretwork, is listed by INAH at 210 pesos general admission, 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and residents, with hours of 8:00 to 17:00 and last access at 16:30.

The Centro Historico carries the museums, the Zocalo and the highest prices. Jalatlaco, a few blocks northeast, is the quieter cobbled quarter with murals and smaller kitchens. Xochimilco, uphill to the north, is residential and calm. Reforma is where longer stay visitors and remote workers concentrate.

Arrival is through Oaxaca International Airport, roughly nine kilometres south of the centre. The official airport colectivo runs 135 pesos to Zone 1 covering the Centro Historico and 210 pesos to Zone 2, while a taxi especial is 490 pesos to Zone 1 and more to Zone 2, with rates posted at the terminal booth. Uber and DiDi remain effectively banned across Oaxaca state as of 2026, so ride hailing is not the fallback it is elsewhere in Mexico.

The calendar is unusually consequential. The dry season runs roughly October to April and the rains fall May to September as afternoon downpours, with June the wettest month. Two events dominate. The Guelaguetza culminates on the Lunes del Cerro at the Auditorio Guelaguetza on Cerro del Fortin, falling on Monday July 20 and Monday July 27 in 2026, with reported prices of 1,476 pesos presale and 1,632 pesos regular for Palco A and 1,166 presale and 1,321 regular for Palco B, while Palcos C and D are free on a first arrival basis. Dia de Muertos runs October 31 to November 2, with the vigils at the Santa Cruz Xoxocotlan cemetery about five kilometres from the centre drawing the largest crowds.

Both peaks come with a real cost. Day of the Dead accommodation is reported at 50 to 80 percent above baseline rates with three to five night minimums, and properties commonly sell out by August or September. Tourism to Oaxaca has risen roughly 77 percent since 2020, and residents have organised protests over short term rentals, housing displacement and water allocation, with reports of neighbourhoods going weeks without running water while hotels stayed supplied. Visitors are arriving into an active local dispute, not a neutral backdrop.

The food and mezcal justify the trip on their own. Mercado 20 de Noviembre and Mercado Benito Juarez sit side by side downtown, and the Sunday market at Tlacolula is worth the drive. On mezcal, the honest warning is that cheap tours are the problem: operators charging under about 30 US dollars per person typically recoup the difference through commission on bottle sales, which forces the palenques in and around Santiago Matatlan to hard sell. Paying more for a smaller group that pays the producer properly is the difference between a distillery visit and a sales pitch.
destinations.what_great: Monte Alban is a levelled mountaintop city with 1,500 years of Olmec, Zapotec and Mixtec occupation, open 8:00 to 17:00 for 210 pesos, and it is 10 kilometres from a colonial grid that shares the same 1987 UNESCO inscription. The Museo de las Culturas at Santo Domingo holds the Tomb 7 Mixtec gold. Mercado 20 de Noviembre and the Sunday Tlacolula market are working markets, not displays. Mitla's stone fretwork, 210 pesos general admission, has no equivalent anywhere in Mexico.
destinations.what_ruined: Festival season breaks the city. Day of the Dead lodging is reported at 50 to 80 percent above baseline with three to five night minimums and properties sold out by August. Guelaguetza box seats run to 1,632 pesos. Tourism is up roughly 77 percent since 2020, and residents have protested short-term rentals, displacement and water allocation, with reports of neighbourhoods dry for weeks while hotels stayed supplied. Mezcal tours under 30 dollars recoup costs by pressuring palenques into hard selling. Hierve el Agua closes unpredictably.
tips: Arrive at Monte Alban at the 8:00 opening, since the site closes at 17:00 with last admission at 16:00 and there is almost no shade on the Gran Plaza.
Skip Monte Alban on Sunday if you want space, because free entry for Mexicans and residents that day makes it the most crowded of the week.
Take the official airport colectivo at 135 pesos to the Centro Historico instead of the 490 peso taxi especial, since both are booked at the same posted-rate terminal booth.
Do not plan on Uber or DiDi, which remain effectively banned across Oaxaca state in 2026, and agree a fare with street taxis before getting in.
Buy Guelaguetza tickets only through SuperBoletos, the sole authorised online vendor, or queue for the free Palco C and D seating on the Lunes del Cerro dates of 20 and 27 July 2026.
Carry cash for Hierve el Agua, where entry is cash only at roughly 50 to 70 pesos plus a community fee and there are no ATMs at the site, and confirm within a week that it has not closed.

guide.title: Oaxaca Practical Guide: OAX Transfers, Monte Alban Fees, Festival Months and Real Budgets
guide.summary: Month by month timing around Guelaguetza and Day of the Dead, official airport transfer rates, current INAH site fees, honest daily budget bands, and the scams worth knowing.
guide.body:
Oaxaca has a dry season from roughly October to April and a rainy season from May to September. The rains are afternoon events rather than all day washouts, with most mornings clear, and June is the wettest month. The most comfortable stretch is late January into early March, when the heat has not built and humidity is at its lowest. May, June, September and early October are the cheapest and quietest months, with lower hotel rates and thinner crowds, at the cost of daily afternoon storms. The two dates that will define your trip and your budget are the Guelaguetza, whose Lunes del Cerro performances at the Auditorio Guelaguetza on Cerro del Fortin fall on Monday July 20 and Monday July 27 in 2026, and Dia de Muertos, which runs October 31 to November 2. Both fill the city. Day of the Dead in particular is reported to push accommodation 50 to 80 percent above baseline with three to five night minimums, with many properties sold out by August or September, so book those months ahead or deliberately choose different dates.

Getting in means Oaxaca International Airport, about nine kilometres south of the centre and 20 to 30 minutes by road. The official airport colectivo, a shared van booked at the terminal booth with posted rates, costs 135 pesos to Zone 1, which covers the Centro Historico, and 210 pesos to Zone 2 for outlying neighbourhoods like San Felipe del Agua. A private taxi especial from the same booth is 490 pesos to Zone 1 and costs more to Zone 2, so check the posted board before you pay. Card payment is accepted at the booth. Plan for the absence of ride hailing: Uber and DiDi remain effectively banned across Oaxaca state as of 2026, so street taxis, the colectivo system and walking are the real options.

Getting around the city is overwhelmingly on foot. The Centro Historico grid is compact and the Andador Macedonio Alcala is pedestrianised. For the valley, colectivos and second class buses leave regularly for Mitla, Tlacolula and Santa Maria del Tule, and a hired driver for a full day of valley sites is the efficient alternative to a group tour.

For sites, Monte Alban is the anchor. Open daily 8:00 to 17:00 with last entry at 16:00, admission is 210 pesos general and 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and residents under the INAH schedule that took effect January 1, 2026. Sundays are free for Mexicans and residents, which is exactly why Sunday is the worst day to go for space and quiet. Get there at opening for shade and empty plazas. The Museo de las Culturas de Oaxaca in the former convent at Santo Domingo is 210 pesos general and 105 for nationals and residents, open Tuesday to Saturday 10:00 to 17:30 with last entry at 17:00 and Sunday 10:00 to 15:30, closed Mondays, and the Tomb 7 Mixtec goldwork inside is genuinely world class. Mitla, 45 kilometres southeast, is listed by INAH at 210 pesos general and 105 pesos for Mexican nationals and residents, 8:00 to 17:00, last access 16:30, and its geometric stone mosaics are unlike anything else in Mexico. Hierve el Agua, the mineral terraces east of the city, is the one to approach with caution: entry is cash only and typically quoted in the range of 50 to 70 pesos plus a small community fee, but the site has closed unpredictably during an ongoing dispute between the co-managing communities, so confirm access within a week of going. The Sunday market at Tlacolula is worth building a day around. The thing to skip is any bargain mezcal tour priced under about 30 US dollars per person.

On budget, the verifiable line items are the airport transfer at 135 to 490 pesos, Monte Alban at 210 pesos, the Santo Domingo museum at 210 pesos and Mitla at 210 pesos. At roughly 18 pesos to the US dollar, that is about 7 to 27 dollars for the transfer and about 12 dollars for each of the three sites. Building outward from those, a realistic daily total is about 45 to 65 dollars for a budget traveller in a hostel or guesthouse eating at Mercado 20 de Noviembre, about 90 to 150 dollars for a mid range visitor in a Centro boutique hotel with restaurant meals and one valley excursion, and 250 dollars and up during Guelaguetza or Dia de Muertos, when lodging alone can consume the entire mid range figure.

On safety, Oaxaca state carries a US State Department Level 2 advisory, exercise increased caution, which is the same tier as much of the country and well below a do not travel designation. The practical risks in the city are petty theft in crowded markets and around festival crowds, and taxi overcharging, which is best managed by agreeing a fare before getting in since meters are uncommon. Carry cash for Hierve el Agua and rural markets, since there are no ATMs at the terraces. The commission driven mezcal tour is the most common commercial trap. Finally, be aware of the local context: tourism is up roughly 77 percent since 2020 and residents have protested over short term rentals, displacement and water access, so occasional demonstrations and road blockages are a genuine possibility rather than a curiosity.

rating_rationale.overall: The 1987 UNESCO listing pairing the colonial centre with Monte Alban, plus a food and mezcal culture with no real equivalent in Mexico, makes this a first-rank destination in almost any month.
rating_rationale.safety: Oaxaca state sits at a US State Department Level 2 advisory, exercise increased caution, with everyday risk in the city limited mainly to petty theft, taxi overcharging and occasional protest-related road blockages.
rating_rationale.value: Site fees are low at 210 pesos for Monte Alban and 210 pesos for Mitla and the airport colectivo is 135 pesos, but Day of the Dead lodging reportedly runs 50 to 80 percent above baseline with multi-night minimums.

destinations.name: Prague
destinations.summary: Prague pairs a UNESCO listed historic core of Gothic, Baroque and Art Nouveau architecture with one of Europe's best beer and pub cultures, though rising visitor numbers pushed the city into new nightlife curfews, a tourist tax fight and a 2026 transit fare increase.
destinations.headline: Prague in 2026: Castle Views, Cheap Beer and a City Cracking Down on Overtourism
destinations.body:
Prague's historic center, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992, remains one of the most architecturally intact old towns in Europe, with Gothic, Baroque and Art Nouveau buildings lining the Vltava River from Prague Castle down through Mala Strana, across Charles Bridge and into Old Town Square. St Vitus Cathedral and the Astronomical Clock anchor the main sightseeing route, while neighborhoods like Vinohrady and Zizkov offer quieter, residential alternatives with their own restaurant and pub scenes away from the main tourist flow.

The city is in the middle of a genuine crackdown on the effects of overtourism. As of January 1, 2026, shared e scooter rentals are banned citywide, organized bar crawls are prohibited between 10pm and 6am, and Prague 1 has designated no drinking zones covering Old Town Square, the Charles Bridge area and Wenceslas Square, where an open container can draw a fine. Prague's municipal tourist tax currently sits at CZK 50 per person per night, but Prague 1's district council has proposed raising it to roughly CZK 175, about EUR 7, to bring it closer to the EU average. A national review board is expected to rule by mid 2026, with any new rate taking effect in 2027.

Getting around got more expensive at the start of 2026. A 30 minute PID transit ticket now costs 39 CZK on paper, or 36 CZK in the PID Litacka app, and a 90 minute ticket costs 50 CZK on paper, or 46 CZK in app, both covering metro, tram, bus and the Petrin funicular with a single validation. The Airport Express bus from Vaclav Havel Airport to Prague's main train station also doubled in price in January 2026, from 100 to 200 CZK for the roughly 35 minute ride.

A day trip to Kutna Hora, about one hour away by train, remains one of the best side trips from Prague, combining the Gothic St Barbara's Cathedral with the Sedlec Ossuary, a chapel decorated with the bones of an estimated 40,000 to 70,000 people. Visitors from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and dozens of other visa exempt countries can currently stay up to 90 days within any 180 day period without a visa. The EU's ETIAS pre travel authorization system is expected to start applying to this group in late 2026.
destinations.what_great: Prague's core appeal is architectural density paired with an unusually good and still affordable food and beer scene. Czech pilsner style lager, hearty pub fare and a real neighborhood life in areas like Vinohrady and Zizkov reward visitors who venture beyond Old Town. The castle complex, Charles Bridge and the Vltava riverfront deliver on the postcard version of the city, and Kutna Hora offers one of the more unusual and worthwhile day trips in Central Europe.
destinations.what_ruined: The honest friction is overcrowding and rising cost. Old Town Square, Charles Bridge and the routes between them are jammed with tour groups for much of the year, and the same few blocks host currency exchange counters running bait and switch rates plus restaurants that pad bills with unlisted service charges, uninvited bread baskets and tip screens defaulting to 20 percent. Transit fares and the airport bus both got meaningfully more expensive in January 2026, and the city's own fight over its tourist tax signals further increases are coming for 2027.
tips: A 90 minute Prague public transit ticket covering metro, tram and bus costs 50 CZK on paper or 46 CZK in the PID Litacka app as of the January 2026 fare increase, and must be validated once at the start of the trip.

The Airport Express bus from Vaclav Havel Airport to Praha hlavni nadrazi costs 200 CZK one way as of January 2026, after the fare was doubled from 100 CZK. Regular Prague transit tickets are not valid on this line.

Prague Castle's main Circuit ticket, covering the Old Royal Palace, St George's Basilica, Golden Lane and St Vitus Cathedral interior, costs 450 CZK for an adult and 300 CZK for a concession. The castle grounds and courtyards are free and open daily from 6am to 10pm.

Citizens of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and roughly 55 other visa exempt countries can stay in the Czech Republic and the wider Schengen area for up to 90 days within any 180 day period without a visa.

At ATMs and card terminals in Prague, always choose to be charged in CZK rather than accepting the machine's offered home currency conversion, known as Dynamic Currency Conversion, which typically carries a 3 to 7 percent hidden markup.
Prague's shared e scooter rental services have been banned citywide since January 1, 2026, and organized bar crawls are prohibited between 10pm and 6am under new city rules.

guide.title: Prague Travel Guide 2026: When to Go, Where to Stay and What to Skip
guide.summary: A practical primer on visiting Prague in 2026, covering transit costs, neighborhood choices, day trips and the scams worth knowing about before landing.
guide.body:
Most visitors fly into Vaclav Havel Airport and take the Airport Express bus, 200 CZK, about 35 minutes, or a metro plus tram combination into the center. Ride hailing apps such as Bolt and Uber are widely available and often cheaper than a taxi hailed at the terminal. Spring, April through June, and early autumn, September and October, offer the best balance of mild weather and manageable crowds, while July and August bring peak heat and the heaviest tour group traffic through Old Town Square and Charles Bridge. Winter is cold but quiet, and Prague Castle's interiors keep shorter hours, 9am to 4pm, from November through March.

For lodging, Old Town and Mala Strana put visitors inside walking distance of the major sights but at premium prices and maximum foot traffic. Vinohrady and Zizkov, both a short tram ride from the center, offer quieter, more residential stays with strong local restaurant and pub scenes at lower cost. Budget travelers can expect to spend meaningfully less than in Paris or Amsterdam, though the January 2026 transit fare increase and the proposed 2027 tourist tax hike are narrowing that gap.

A single 90 minute PID transit ticket, 50 CZK on paper or 46 CZK via the PID Litacka app, covers the metro, trams and buses citywide and must be validated once at the start of the ride. Must do sightseeing includes Prague Castle and St Vitus Cathedral, the Astronomical Clock in Old Town Square, and an early morning walk across Charles Bridge before the crowds arrive. A worthwhile day trip is Kutna Hora, about one hour away by train, for the Sedlec Ossuary and St Barbara's Cathedral. What to avoid: currency exchange counters and restaurants directly on Old Town Square, Charles Bridge and Wenceslas Square, where bait exchange rates and padded restaurant bills are well documented. Eating and exchanging money one street back, on streets such as Dlouha or Dusni, avoids most of it.

rating_rationale.overall: Prague delivers fully on its architectural and cultural reputation, but heavy crowding in the historic core and a fast changing fee landscape keep it just short of a perfect score.
rating_rationale.safety: Violent crime against tourists is rare in Prague, but well documented currency exchange and restaurant overcharging scams are frequent enough in the main tourist zones to warrant real caution.
rating_rationale.value: Prague remains cheaper than most Western European capitals, but the January 2026 transit fare hike, the doubled airport bus fare and a looming tourist tax increase are steadily narrowing that gap.

facts_checked: Prague's municipal tourist tax is currently CZK 50 per person per night; Prague 1's district council has proposed raising it to about CZK 175, roughly EUR 7, with a national decision expected by mid 2026 and a new rate effective 2027 if approved. Source: expats.cz coverage of the Prague 1 tourist tax proposal.

Shared e scooter rentals have been banned citywide since January 1, 2026; organized bar crawls are banned between 10pm and 6am; no drinking zones now cover Old Town Square, the Charles Bridge area and Wenceslas Square. Source: 2026 Prague overtourism coverage on bestpragueguide.com and dreamville.cz.

The 30 minute PID transit ticket costs 39 CZK on paper or 36 CZK in the PID Litacka app; the 90 minute ticket costs 50 CZK on paper or 46 CZK in app, effective January 1, 2026. Source: e15.cz Czech finance and transit reporting on the 2026 PID fare increase.
The Airport Express bus fare was doubled from 100 CZK to 200 CZK in January 2026, for the roughly 35 minute ride from the airport to Praha hlavni nadrazi with no transfers. Source: Prague Daily News.

Prague Castle's Circuit ticket costs 450 CZK for an adult, 300 CZK concession, 950 CZK for a family; the Tower of the Cathedral view gallery costs 200 CZK for an adult; the grounds are free and open daily 6am to 10pm, with interiors open 9am to 5pm in summer and 9am to 4pm in winter. Source: timetravelturtle.com and thebettervacation.com 2026 Prague Castle ticket guides.

Visa exempt visitors, including from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, may stay up to 90 days within any 180 day period in the Schengen area including Czechia; the EU's ETIAS pre travel authorization is expected to begin applying to this group in late 2026. Source: europe-visa.eu and axa-schengen.com.

Currency exchange scams are common near Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square, and ATM Dynamic Currency Conversion carries a 3 to 7 percent markup; travelers should always choose to be charged in CZK. Source: bestpragueguide.com Prague scams guide.

Restaurant overcharging in tourist zones near Old Town Square, Charles Bridge and Wenceslas Square includes added service charges, uninvited bread or snacks billed later, and payment terminal tip screens defaulting to 20 percent. Source: prague-guide.co.uk and tabiji.ai.
Kutna Hora is about one hour from Prague by train and is home to the Gothic St Barbara's Cathedral, begun in 1388, and the Sedlec Ossuary bone chapel. Source: skysonar.com Prague itinerary guide.

destinations.name: Queenstown
destinations.summary: Lakeside resort town on Lake Wakatipu in New Zealand's South Island, built around commercial adventure tourism, alpine scenery and winter skiing.
destinations.headline: Queenstown Is Worth Seeing And Expensive To Do: NZ$199 Jet Boats, NZ$320 Bungy, NZ$100 Levy
destinations.body:
Queenstown occupies a shelf of land on the northeastern shore of Lake Wakatipu, hemmed in by The Remarkables to the southeast and Ben Lomond directly above the town centre. It is compact, roughly a fifteen minute walk end to end, with the town centre and Queenstown Bay at its heart, the residential and commercial sprawl of Frankton eight kilometres east near the airport, and Fernhill and Sunshine Bay strung west along the lake. Arrowtown, a preserved gold-rush settlement, sits about twenty kilometres northeast, the Gibbston Valley wine district lies through the Kawarau Gorge, and Glenorchy is at the head of the lake, a spectacular forty-five minute drive that is a genuine highlight and costs nothing.

Arriving is now a taxed process. Most international visitors pay the International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy of NZ$100, charged at the same time as an NZeTA request or visa application, and the NZeTA itself starts at NZ$17 through the official Immigration New Zealand app and is valid for two years. Australian citizens, New Zealanders and some Pacific nationals are exempt from the levy. Both charges are non-refundable and neither guarantees entry. There is no local bed tax: Queenstown Lakes residents voted more than 80 percent in favour of a visitor levy in a non-binding 2019 referendum, but the legislation was never enacted and the proposal remains on hold.

Queenstown Airport is one of the closest airports to a town centre in the country, and the Orbus public network makes the transfer trivially cheap. An adult airport fare is NZ$2.50 with a Bee Card or NZ$10 in cash, and standard adult fares elsewhere on the network are NZ$2.50 with a Bee Card or NZ$4 cash. The Bee Card costs NZ$5 with a NZ$5 minimum top-up, which breaks even against the NZ$10 cash airport fare on the first trip and saves on every trip after it, so buy one immediately.

The headline activities are priced accordingly. The Skyline Gondola up Bob's Peak is NZ$69 for an adult and NZ$48 for a child, a gondola plus three luge rides package is NZ$99 adult, and gondola with unlimited luge is NZ$140. Shotover Jet, the jet boat operation in the Shotover River canyons, is NZ$199 adult, NZ$109 for children aged five to fifteen and NZ$507 for a family pass. AJ Hackett's Kawarau Bridge Bungy, the original commercial bungy site, starts at NZ$320 for an adult and NZ$280 for a child, with photos, video and a T-shirt included when booked direct. Combination packages escalate quickly, with the bungy, swing and zipline trio at NZ$495 and a Kawarau plus Nevis bungy combo at NZ$615. A RealNZ coach and cruise day trip to Milford Sound starts at NZ$292, involves five hours of coach travel each way plus a cruise of up to two hours, and departs between 6.45am and 7.35am.

Seasons are sharply defined. The southern winter, roughly mid-June to early October, is ski season at Coronet Peak and The Remarkables and the town's busiest, most expensive period. December to February brings warm, long days, hiking on the Ben Lomond and Queenstown Hill tracks, and heavy domestic and international crowds. April to May and October to November are the shoulder seasons with the best price-to-crowd ratio. Whatever the month, expect traffic: Frankton Road exceeded ten million vehicle trips in 2025, and a NZ$250 million upgrade of the State Highway 6 and 6A Frankton intersection began in April 2024 and runs for around four years.
destinations.what_great: The landscape does the heavy lifting and much of it is free: the Queenstown Gardens peninsula, the Frankton Track along the lake, Queenstown Hill and the Glenorchy road all cost nothing. Adventure operators are professionally run under New Zealand's adventure activity regime, so the risk is managed rather than pretended away. Orbus fares of NZ$2.50 with a Bee Card make getting around genuinely cheap. Arrowtown, Gibbston Valley wineries and the Kawarau Gorge are all within thirty minutes.
destinations.what_ruined: Cost is the defining complaint. NZ$199 for a jet boat ride, NZ$320 to start a bungy and NZ$292 for a Milford day trip means a couple can burn NZ$1,000 in a single day without eating. Accommodation prices spike hard through ski season and midsummer, and the shortage of housing keeps a floor under rates all year. The town centre saturates in peak months, restaurant waits are long, and Frankton Road, one of New Zealand's busiest single-carriageway roads, jams daily while a four-year intersection rebuild runs until roughly 2028.
tips: Pay the NZ$100 International Visitor Levy and request the NZeTA from NZ$17 through the official Immigration New Zealand app before you fly, because both are required and non-refundable.
Buy a NZ$5 Bee Card on arrival, since it drops the airport bus fare from NZ$10 cash to NZ$2.50 and cuts every other Orbus trip to NZ$2.50.
If you only do one paid attraction, the Skyline Gondola at NZ$69 adult gives the town's defining view, and adding three luge rides brings it to NZ$99.
Book the Milford Sound day trip from NZ$292 knowing it is five hours of coach each way with departures from 6.45am, so it consumes an entire day.
Travel in April, May, October or November to avoid both the mid-June to early October ski peak and the December to February summer crush.
Allow well over the map estimate for any drive through Frankton, because the NZ$250 million SH6/SH6A intersection rebuild started in April 2024 and runs about four years.

guide.title: Queenstown Guide: Entry Levies, Airport Bus Fares, Real Activity Prices And Budgets
guide.summary: Month-by-month timing, the NZ$100 levy and NZeTA, cheap Orbus transfers from the airport, verified activity prices, a realistic daily budget in US dollars, and safety realities.
guide.body:
Start with the paperwork, because New Zealand now charges for it. Most international visitors must pay the International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy of NZ$100, collected at the same moment you request an NZeTA or apply for a visa. The NZeTA starts at NZ$17 through the official Immigration New Zealand mobile app, costs more if requested through the website, and is valid for two years for travellers. Australian and New Zealand passport holders, several Pacific nationalities, transit passengers at Auckland and holders of certain resident and business visitor visas are exempt from the levy. Both charges are non-refundable, and neither guarantees admission at the border. There is no separate Queenstown bed tax despite a 2019 non-binding referendum in which more than 80 percent of Queenstown Lakes voters supported a five percent accommodation levy; the local bill stalled and the proposal has not been enacted.

On timing, Queenstown has two peaks and two good shoulders. Mid-June to early October is ski season, with Coronet Peak and The Remarkables driving demand and pushing accommodation to its annual highs. December through February brings long, warm days, the Ben Lomond and Queenstown Hill tracks in full use and the largest overall visitor volume. April and May, and again October and November, are the shoulders, when the weather is variable but crowds thin and prices soften. Autumn colour through Arrowtown in April is genuinely worth planning around. Whatever the month, alpine weather changes fast and the Milford Road can close, so build slack into any fixed schedule.

Getting in from Queenstown Airport is the easiest and cheapest part of the trip. The airport sits at Frankton, roughly eight kilometres from the town centre, and the Otago Regional Council's Orbus network serves it directly with onward connections through the Frankton Bus Interchange. An adult airport fare is NZ$2.50 with a Bee Card or NZ$10 in cash, and child and youth fares are NZ$1.50 with a Bee Card or NZ$8 cash. Off the airport route, standard adult fares are NZ$2.50 with a Bee Card and NZ$4 cash, with child and youth at NZ$1.50 by card. The Bee Card itself costs NZ$5 and requires a NZ$5 minimum top-up, which exactly breaks even against the NZ$10 cash airport fare on the first ride and saves from the second onward. Taxis, rideshare and private shuttles all operate from the terminal at conventional resort-town prices. A rental car is only worth it if you intend to drive to Glenorchy, Arrowtown, Wanaka or the Milford Road, because parking in the town centre is limited and expensive.

On what to do, the Skyline Gondola to Bob's Peak is the signature and costs NZ$69 for an adult and NZ$48 for a child, with adults counted from 15 and children from 6 to 14. A gondola plus three luge rides is NZ$99 adult and NZ$68 child, and gondola with unlimited luge is NZ$140 adult. A three-day unlimited gondola upgrade is NZ$34.50 adult, which is good value for anyone staying a while. Shotover Jet runs the canyon jet boat trips at NZ$199 adult, NZ$109 for children aged 5 to 15 and NZ$507 for a family pass covering two adults and two children. AJ Hackett's Kawarau Bridge Bungy, the world's first commercial bungy site, starts at NZ$320 adult and NZ$280 child, including photos, video and a T-shirt when booked direct, and combos run to NZ$460 for bungy and swing, NZ$495 with the zipline added and NZ$615 for a Kawarau plus Nevis day. The RealNZ Milford Sound day trip from Queenstown starts at NZ$292, with coach travel of five hours each way and a cruise of up to two hours, departing at 6.45am, 6.55am or 7.35am. If the budget is tight, skip the paid attractions entirely: the Queenstown Gardens loop, the Frankton Track, Queenstown Hill and the drive to Glenorchy are free and arguably deliver more scenery per hour than anything ticketed.

On budget, a genuinely lean trip staying in hostels, self-catering and doing free walks runs roughly 90 to 130 US dollars per person per day. A mid-range trip with a modest hotel or motel room, restaurant dinners, bus fares and one paid activity every second day runs roughly 220 to 340 dollars per person per day. Add a single flagship activity and the day jumps: the jet boat alone is about 120 US dollars and the Kawarau bungy about 190. A family of four doing gondola, luge and a jet boat in one day will clear 700 US dollars before food. Accommodation is the least predictable line, spiking hardest through ski season and the Christmas to February window, and the district's chronic housing shortage keeps rates elevated even in the shoulders.

Queenstown has little violent crime; what actually hurts visitors here is the terrain and the roads, not other people. Commercial adventure operators work under New Zealand's adventure activity regulations with audited safety systems, which is why the bungy and jet boat operations have the records they do, so choose licensed operators and follow briefings rather than improvising. Alpine weather turns quickly on the Ben Lomond track and around the ski fields, so carry layers and check forecasts. Driving is the bigger hazard: the roads to Glenorchy, Milford and over the Crown Range are narrow, winding and often icy in winter, and visitors unfamiliar with driving on the left are overrepresented in crashes. Allow far more time than mapping apps suggest, particularly around Frankton, where the road exceeded ten million vehicle trips in 2025 and a NZ$250 million rebuild of the SH6 and SH6A intersection has been under construction since April 2024. Petty theft from parked cars at trailheads does happen, so leave nothing visible.

rating_rationale.overall: The setting and the depth of professionally run adventure operators are world class, but the town itself is small, congested and increasingly shaped around extracting spend from visitors.
rating_rationale.safety: Crime against visitors is minimal and adventure operators work under strict New Zealand adventure activity regulation, leaving alpine driving and weather as the main genuine risks.
rating_rationale.value: A single jet boat ride is NZ$199 and a Kawarau bungy starts at NZ$320, so a family can spend more in one afternoon here than on several days elsewhere in New Zealand.
